author.name: Daniele Zago

entry.content:
The paper “Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses suspected of inflicting deliberate harm on patients” by Prof. John O’Quigley explores an interesting hypothesis concerning statistical information hidden in the part of the infamous Lucy Letby roster chart pertaining to the 37 other nurses. Unfortunately, we have to point out some serious errors in his statistical analyses. The data actually contains information which strongly disproves his main modelling assumption. We do, however, strongly agree with him that from a forensic statistical point of view, the roster chart is fake evidence which should not have been shown to jurors.

Read more

author.name: Daniele Zago

entry.title: A Bayesian Magnitude-Composition Model for Tree-Size Distributions and Stand-Tables

link.title: A Bayesian Magnitude-Composition Model for Tree-Size Distributions and Stand-Tables

entry.content:
Sparse forest inventories often provide too few plots to estimate species-specific tree-size distributions for individual stands. We develop a general Bayesian magnitude-composition model that separates overall abundance from its allocation among categories. A negative-binomial model describes total counts, while multinomial models describe how those counts are allocated among categories. In forest inventory, this construction allocates trees among species and then size classes within species, without imposing a parametric form on the tree-size distribution. Covariates inform both abundance and composition. Shared latent factors represent residual spatial and group-level dependence among categories using relatively few processes, while smoothing priors on regression coefficients borrow information across neighboring size classes. Nearest-neighbor Gaussian processes support efficient spatial computation. Joint posterior prediction and area-weighted aggregation yield stand-tables—tree densities by species and size class—and derived measures such as size-class diversity, with associated uncertainty. Simulations show small estimation errors and near-nominal predictive-interval coverage for forest and stand summaries. An application combining field plots and light detection and ranging (LiDAR) covariates illustrates estimation of species-specific distributions of diameter at breast height and size-class diversity in sampled and unsampled stands.

Read more

entry.title: A Bayesian quantile mixed model for bounded discrete outcomes

link.title: A Bayesian quantile mixed model for bounded discrete outcomes

entry.content:
Quantile regression for longitudinal bounded integer outcomes must accommodate discreteness, finite support, and dependence within participants. We develop a Bayesian quantile mixed model using a discrete Kumaraswamy distribution parameterized through a smooth quantile anchor whose ceiling gives the corresponding integer quantile. Covariates and correlated Gaussian participant effects enter a logit predictor for the scaled anchor, while a separate regression models distributional shape. Posterior computation combines a conjugate Gaussian coefficient update, available for compatible fixed and random effect designs, with slice sampling and covariance interweaving. Simulations showed small biases in regression coefficients and generally near-nominal coverage of 95% credible intervals. An application to repeated cognitive scores illustrates covariate associations across separately fitted quantile levels. Posterior predictive checks captured broad distributional patterns.

Read more

entry.title: A Beta-Based Heteroskedasticity-Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimator

link.title: A Beta-Based Heteroskedasticity-Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimator

entry.content:
This paper introduces an adaptive leverage correction for heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimation in ordinary least squares regression. Unlike existing estimators, which rely on predetermined adjustment functions, the proposed approach uses a fitted Beta distribution calibrated to the design matrix’s empirical leverage structure. Its parameters are estimated from observed leverage values, allowing the adjustment to reflect the overall configuration rather than individual values alone. The estimator accommodates heterogeneous leverage patterns while avoiding excessive growth of adjustment factors. Monte Carlo simulations show accurate finite-sample inference and confidence interval coverage, alongside desirable asymptotic properties. Empirical applications illustrate its advantages with influential observations and overshooting by existing estimators. The open-source R package hcinfer implements the estimator and related procedures.

Read more

entry.title: A Debiased Machine Learning Single-Imputation Framework for Item Nonresponse in Surveys

link.title: A Debiased Machine Learning Single-Imputation Framework for Item Nonresponse in Surveys

entry.content:
Machine-learning methods offer flexible alternatives to parametric models for imputing missing survey values. However, using their predictions in the customary imputed estimator does not automatically yield valid inference. We explain why the error from estimating the regression function can prevent root-$n$ consistency and develop inference for a finite population mean using a cross-fitted augmented inverse-probability-weighted (AIPW) estimator. The analysis combines an imputation model, a sampling design, and a missing-at-random response mechanism, while allowing dependence among sampling indicators. We establish double robustness and show that, under suitable regularity conditions, consistency of both nuisance estimators together with a product-rate condition yields oracle equivalence and asymptotic normality. We also derive consistent variance estimators accounting for sampling and nonresponse. To obtain a completed survey variable, we construct adjusted imputed values that preserve observed responses and whose weighted mean reproduces the AIPW estimate exactly. We further discuss aggregation of nuisance learners and the conditions under which it preserves the prediction rates needed for inference. Simulations show that cross-fitting can substantially reduce undercoverage, but may increase mean squared error when nuisance predictions are inaccurate.

Read more

entry.title: A General Approach for Assessing Sensitivity to Violations of Causal Assumptions

link.title: A General Approach for Assessing Sensitivity to Violations of Causal Assumptions

entry.content:
Although causal sensitivity analyses are widely used to assess the robustness of conclusions, a key limitation is that existing methods are typically developed for specific designs. This paper develops a general sensitivity analysis framework that applies to a wide range of discrete causal models and estimands by deriving sharp bounds on causal estimands as a function of the maximum proportion of the population for which the assumption is relaxed. The framework is built on the generalized principal strata approach, which allows the translation of assumptions, estimands, and data into polynomial programs. In this approach, three classes of assumptions can be relaxed: a) functional restrictions, which limit the ways that one variable can respond to another, e.g. strong monotonicity; b) exclusion restrictions, which rule out direct causal effects; c) unconfoundedness, which rules out unobserved common causes of variables. The approach produces both sharp sensitivity curves and robustness values, i.e., the smallest sensitivity level at which the sign of a causal effect stops being identified. The applicability of the method is demonstrated by generalizing existing proportion-of-violations approaches, deriving new sensitivity analysis methods for instrumental variable and selection-on-observables designs, and reanalyzing empirical results.

Read more

entry.title: A Generalized Tangent Approximation based Variational Inference Framework for Strongly Super-Gaussian Likelihoods

link.title: A Generalized Tangent Approximation based Variational Inference Framework for Strongly Super-Gaussian Likelihoods

entry.content:
Variational inference, as an alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, has played a transformative role in enabling scalable computation for complex Bayesian models. Nevertheless, existing approaches often depend on either rigid model-specific formulations or stochastic black-box optimization routines. Tangent approximation is a principled class of structured variational methods that exploit the geometry of the underlying probability model. However, its utility has largely been confined to logistic regression and related modeling regimes. In this article, we propose a novel variational framework based on tangent transformation for a broad class of probability models characterized by strongly super-Gaussian likelihoods. Our method leverages convex duality to construct tangent minorants of the log-likelihood, thereby inducing conjugacy with Gaussian priors over model parameters in an otherwise intractable setup. Under mild assumptions on the data-generating mechanism, we establish algorithmic convergence guarantees, a contribution that stands in contrast to the limited theoretical assurances typically available for black-box variational methods. Additionally, we derive near-parametric variational risk bounds. Superior performance of our proposed methodology is illustrated on simulated and real-data scenarios that challenge state-of-the-art variational algorithms in terms of scalability and their ability to consistently capture complex underlying data structure.

Read more

entry.title: A Kernel-Based Test for Multi-Way Conditional Independence

link.title: A Kernel-Based Test for Multi-Way Conditional Independence

entry.content:
Conditional independence involving more than two variables, or multi-way conditional independence, is a fundamental probabilistic structure useful in many areas of statistical research, including latent-variable and graphical models. However, most existing works focus on pairwise conditional independence. To address this gap, we propose a kernel-based test of multi-way conditional independence. Specifically, we characterize this hypothesis through the simultaneous vanishing of a vector of conditional cross-covariance operators and construct a test statistic based on the norm of the vector of their estimators. We derive the statistic’s asymptotic distributions under the null hypothesis and local alternatives. As a related methodological contribution, we also develop a test of multi-way unconditional independence and provide a procedure for its implementation. An application to RNA data illustrates the method’s use in genomics.

Read more

entry.title: A Kernel Nonconformity Score for Multivariate Conformal Prediction

link.title: A Kernel Nonconformity Score for Multivariate Conformal Prediction

entry.content:
Multivariate conformal prediction requires nonconformity scores that compress residual vectors into scalars while preserving certain implicit geometric structure of the residual distribution. We introduce a Multivariate Kernel Score (MKS) that produces prediction regions that explicitly adapt to this geometry. We show that the proposed score resembles the Gaussian process posterior variance, unifying Bayesian uncertainty quantification with the coverage guarantees of frequentist-type. Moreover, the MKS can be decomposed into an anisotropic Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) that interpolates between kernel density estimation and covariance-weighted distance. We prove finite-sample coverage guarantees and establish convergence rates that depend on the effective rank of the kernel-based covariance operator rather than the ambient dimension, enabling dimension-free adaptation. On regression tasks, the MKS reduces the volume of prediction regions significantly, compared to ellipsoidal baselines while maintaining nominal coverage, with larger gains at higher dimensions and tighter coverage levels.

Read more

entry.title: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs

link.title: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs

entry.content:
We study the design of multi-arm experiments that identify local average treatment effects under imperfect compliance. With three or more arms, conventional randomization fails to identify margin-specific effects even under strong extensions of monotone compliance. A choice-theoretic analysis unifies these extensions and motivates a two-stage design: subjects report a preferred arm and are randomized conditional on it. If treatment is confined to the assigned or reported arm, one-sided noncompliance is restored conditional on the report, identifying the effect between the two arms for their compliers. Any tilt of assignment toward the reported arm makes reporting the favorite strictly optimal, and no assignment lottery can strictly elicit the ranking below the favorite. We then discuss the design’s applicability and feasibility in relation to the choice model.

Read more

entry.title: ALDER: A Single-Loop Augmented-Lagrangian Damped Extragradient Method for Nonconvex–Concave Minimax Problems with Nonlinear Coupled Constraints

link.title: ALDER: A Single-Loop Augmented-Lagrangian Damped Extragradient Method for Nonconvex–Concave Minimax Problems with Nonlinear Coupled Constraints

entry.content:
ALDER, a single-loop augmented-Lagrangian damped extragradient method, is proposed for smooth nonconvex–concave minimax problems with nonlinear coupled inequality constraints. Within an augmented-Lagrangian framework, ALDER combines prediction–correction steps for the primal variables with explicit projected-and-relaxed multiplier updates in a single loop. The penalty parameter is fixed throughout each run, eliminating inner-loop subproblem solves and iterative penalty updates. We establish uniform boundedness of the relaxed multiplier sequence and, under an extended Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification, boundedness of the projected output multiplier. Building on these bounds, we show that ALDER finds an $\varepsilon$-KKT point within $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-7/2})$ complete first-order oracle evaluations in the strongly concave setting and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ in the concave setting. These bounds improve upon the best known complexity bounds for multi-loop algorithms for this problem class, achieved by FAL, by removing a $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ factor, while retaining a single-loop update structure.

Read more

entry.title: AQBuc: Air Pollution Forecasting in Bucharest

link.title: AQBuc: Air Pollution Forecasting in Bucharest

entry.content:
In recent years, air pollution, especially the particulate matter $2.5\,\mu\text{m}$ (PM2.5), has become a growing concern mainly in urban areas. Exposure to air pollution is linked to the development of numerous health conditions, such as the aggravation of respiratory diseases, cardiovascular disorders, impaired lung function, and even cancer or early death. Forecasting future levels of PM2.5 has become increasingly important, as it can provide early warnings and help prevent diseases. We propose AQBuc, a dataset for predicting PM2.5 pollution in Bucharest, Romania, introducing an understudied location, as most work in this field has focused on Asian cities. Our dataset allows us to benchmark models for predicting future levels of PM2.5 across various time horizons. We evaluate a broad range of methods, including machine learning models, such as linear regression and ensemble-based methods, deep learning models based on recurrent networks and transformers, and large language models (LLMs). Specialized time-series models handle temporal data better, especially on longer horizons, while tree ensembles are more cost-effective for short horizons. Meanwhile, LLMs struggle to capture continuous sensor dynamics without specialized architectural changes.

Read more

entry.title: A Scientific Claim Stability Framework for Evaluating MRI Morphometry Pipelines

link.title: A Scientific Claim Stability Framework for Evaluating MRI Morphometry Pipelines

entry.content:
MRI morphometry pipelines are often evaluated by measurement agreement or downstream accuracy, yet their scientific value depends on the conclusions they support. Two pipelines can produce similar feature-level results yet support different conclusions about aging, cognitive decline, or neurodegeneration. We introduce Scientific Claim Stability (SCS), a claim-centric evaluation framework that converts region-of-interest (ROI) morphometry tables into auditable claim cards and evaluates their support under changes in dataset, processing pipeline, atlas, feature family, and target. Across 10,370 MRI scans from three datasets and five cohorts, SCS generates 2,783 claim cards and evaluates 89 claim-family pairs. The evaluation distinguishes stable, transferable, and fragile claims. FreeSurfer 8-FastSurfer comparisons show high evidence concordance and low anatomical-support overlap under the primary covariate specification. Acquisition-adjusted analyses show that the magnitude of support disagreement depends on the model specification. Structured review by specialists in geriatrics, neuroscience, and radiology, alongside auxiliary ChatGPT and Gemini reviewers, assesses claim plausibility, clarity, faithfulness, usefulness, and caution. SCS provides a reproducible way to audit the evidential stability of morphometry claims without assuming a universal gold standard.

Read more

entry.title: Abstention Spends Its Budget on Local Label Variance More Than on Novelty: Auditing Conformal Calibration and Selective Prediction under Molecular Scaffold Shift

link.title: Abstention Spends Its Budget on Local Label Variance More Than on Novelty: Auditing Conformal Calibration and Selective Prediction under Molecular Scaffold Shift

entry.content:
Selective prediction with split conformal calibration promises a post-hoc fix for molecular property prediction: abstain on the least reliable compounds, ideally out-of-distribution chemistry, and the retained set becomes trustworthy without retraining. We audit this recipe for a gradient-boosted fingerprint model on lipophilicity (regression) and BBBP (classification) under a Bemis-Murcko scaffold split, holding the fitted model and evaluation molecules fixed while varying only the calibration fold (18 replicates). (i) On lipophilicity, coverage depends on calibration provenance: calibrating on held-out training-scaffold molecules falls below nominal (PICP 0.841 at a 0.90 target), while novel-scaffold calibration recovers it (0.904); on BBBP, coverage stays above nominal in every regime. (ii) For split conformalized quantile regression (CQR) the conformal correction is a constant, so conformalization does not change what is abstained on. (iii) The abstention score (CQR width; effectively ensemble variance on BBBP) tracks local label variance more than chemical novelty: controlling for local label variance largely explains away the novelty association (partial Spearman 0.067 and 0.047). (iv) At a fixed assay budget, gating on interval width or ensemble variance never improves hit precision over ranking by point prediction, at the pre-specified operating point or across 20 exploratory settings; a plain novelty gate shows small, uncorrected gains at the smallest budgets. (v) In an exploratory analysis, exact conformal selection exceeds its false discovery rate target under training-scaffold calibration (0.303 at q=0.2) and is consistent with it under novel-scaffold calibration, contributing a data-driven batch size rather than a better ranking. Conformalization earns its keep through guarantees whose validity hinges on calibration provenance, not by choosing what to abstain on.

Read more

entry.title: Accelerating posterior sampling in Bayesian inverse problems with diffusion models: an online-offline perspective

link.title: Accelerating posterior sampling in Bayesian inverse problems with diffusion models: an online-offline perspective

entry.content:
Bayesian inverse problems require both informative prior models and computationally feasible posterior inference. Score-based diffusion models provide expressive learned priors, but their use for inversion introduces a conditioning problem: the score of a noised posterior is generally unavailable from a prior score alone. This selective survey reviews the principal approaches to that problem, including likelihood guidance, spectral and projection methods, sequential Monte Carlo corrections, and amortized conditional training. We organize methods by how they split cost between offline preparation and online inference, and compare their assumptions, advantages and limitations, with emphasis on computational speedups. Some ongoing directions and open questions are gathered at the end.

Read more

entry.title: Accuracy Is Not Risk: Why Medical AI Should Not Report Only Its Most Likely Label

link.title: Accuracy Is Not Risk: Why Medical AI Should Not Report Only Its Most Likely Label

entry.content:
Background. Many medical AI models are trained to reproduce a single reference label and hand the most likely label to the next step in a clinical workflow. A classifier can select that label correctly while providing an inadequate summary for estimating downstream risk. Methods. We use Jeffrey’s rule of conditioning to specify when probabilities over intermediate states, such as diagnoses or imaging categories, can be carried forward to an outcome risk. We separate two errors of reporting only the most likely label, discarding the probability of the other states and applying the risk of patients who have the leading diagnosis to a patient who only probably has it. We also give conditions under which the label and the full distribution lead to the same decision, and we propose guardrails for device developers, regulatory reviewers, and health insurers. Results. In a hypothetical chest-pain differential, reporting only the benign leading diagnosis greatly understates the patient’s risk of death or cardiac arrest, so a patient who warrants evaluation could be discharged or denied imaging. In a hypothetical BI-RADS example, the most likely category is “probably benign,” yet the propagated malignancy risk exceeds the ceiling that defines that category. Conclusions. A predicted label is not an observed state, and a calibrated classifier is not automatically a valid outcome model. Clinical and insurance coverage decisions should rest on the patient’s outcome risk, judged against a threshold justified by the consequences of acting and not acting. Developers should state what each model output means and check that every step between the model and the decision preserves the patient’s risk.

author.name: Jeffrey Humpherys, Makoto Jones

entry.summary: Background. Many medical AI models are trained to reproduce a single reference label and hand the most likely label to the next step in a clinical workflow. A classifier can select that label correctly while providing an inadequate summary for estimating downstream risk. Methods. We use Jeffrey’s rule of conditioning to specify when probabilities over intermediate states, such as diagnoses or imaging categories, can be carried forward to an outcome risk. We separate two errors of reporting only the most likely label, discarding the probability of the other states and applying the risk of patients who have the leading diagnosis to a patient who only probably has it. We also give conditions under which the label and the full distribution lead to the same decision, and we propose guardrails for device developers, regulatory reviewers, and health insurers. Results. In a hypothetical chest-pain differential, reporting only the benign leading diagnosis greatly understates the patient’s risk of death or cardiac arrest, so a patient who warrants evaluation could be discharged or denied imaging. In a hypothetical BI-RADS example, the most likely category is “probably benign,” yet the propagated malignancy risk exceeds the ceiling that defines that category. Conclusions. Developers should state what each model output means and check that every step between the model and the decision preserves the patient’s risk.

entry.title: Adapting Altman’s bankruptcy prediction model to the compositional data methodology

link.title: Adapting Altman’s bankruptcy prediction model to the compositional data methodology

entry.content:
Using standard financial ratios as variables in statistical analyses has been related to several serious problems, such as extreme outliers, asymmetry, non-normality, and nonlinearity. The compositional-data methodology has been successfully applied to solve these problems and has always yielded substantially different results when compared to standard financial ratios. An under-researched area is the use of financial log-ratios computed with the compositional-data methodology to predict bankruptcy or the related terms of business default, insolvency or failure. Another under-researched area is the use of machine learning methods in combination with compositional log-ratios. The present article adapts the classical Altman bankruptcy prediction model and some of its extensions to the compositional methodology with pairwise log-ratios and three common statistical and machine learning tools: logistic regression models, k-nearest neighbours, and random forests, and compares the results with standard financial ratios. Data from the sector in the Spanish economy with the largest number of bankrupt firms according to the first two digits of the NACE code (46XX “wholesale trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles”) were obtained from the Iberian Balance sheet Analysis System. The sample size (31,131 firms, of which 97 were bankrupt) was divided into a training and a validation dataset. The training dataset was downsampled to one healthy firm to each bankrupt firm. No outliers were removed. Focusing on predictive performance, the results show that compositional methods are better than standard ratios in terms of sensitivity (recall), with mixed results regarding specificity, compositional random forests and compositional logistic regression behaving the best.

Read more

entry.title: Adaptive Optimizers Can Get a Policy Ranking Wrong: Momentum, Dependent Data, and a Two-Run Remedy

link.title: Adaptive Optimizers Can Get a Policy Ranking Wrong: Momentum, Dependent Data, and a Two-Run Remedy

entry.content:
Operators choosing among decision rules, such as when a battery charges or where an idle taxi goes, rank them by estimated long-run value. A standard estimator, linear temporal-difference (TD) learning, fits values from one stream of correlated observations. Large fits often use an adaptive optimizer, such as adaptive moment estimation (Adam), with fixed averaging rates. We show that these rates can change what is estimated, not just how fast: the same observations drive the updates and the optimizer’s step-size scaling, moving the fit away from the intended TD value. The shift differs across rules, so it need not cancel in a comparison, and more data only makes a wrong ranking look more certain. Our remedy refits the same data at a second averaging rate that halves the effective gain, the number to which the leading shift is proportional. Twice the new fit minus the original removes that shift. In New York taxi and battery models calibrated to real data, common optimizer settings leave the selected rule unchanged but order close rules wrongly and misstate its value. Our remedy corrects nearly every wrong ordering, with one extra fit when the shift is moderate and two when it is larger.

Read more

entry.title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms

link.title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms

entry.content:
Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent anytime-valid envelopes do, but deterministic ones are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each concerned with a specific algorithm and a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for sharp, data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for a large class of iterative algorithms. Our approach has two key steps: an optimization module derives a one-step recursion that performance measures of many such algorithms satisfy, reducing the error analysis to time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. Then, a statistical module ports the sub-$\psi$ condition to vector-valued processes, uniformly over predictable weights, and derives off-the-shelf boundaries via mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. Combining the two yields readymade envelopes for many iterative algoithms including but not limited to stochastic gradient descent (SGD), Oja’s algorithm, temporal difference learning, Q-learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD, many with no prior data-adaptive anytime-valid guarantees. Specifically, for SGD, our framework recovers, often under weaker conditions, or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.

Read more

entry.title: A model-based adaptive sampling framework for infectious disease surveillance

link.title: A model-based adaptive sampling framework for infectious disease surveillance

entry.content:
Longitudinal surveillance must choose each round’s sampling design before the next observations arrive. Fixed sample-size rules treat each round as an isolated cross-sectional survey and ignore the evolving uncertainty in the epidemic process, which changes as transmission, vaccination, interventions, variants, and behavior change. We present a model-based adaptive sampling framework for choosing the next-round design. A state-space model represents the epidemic process and maps latent states to surveillance estimands. A statistical filter calibrates the model as observations arrive, propagating uncertainty in latent states, time-varying parameters, stochastic dynamics, and sampling noise. A Bayesian assurance criterion converts the one-step-ahead predictive distribution into the minimum-cost design likely to achieve a target posterior credible-interval width. We evaluated the framework in two simulations and in a retrospective case study of SARS-CoV-2 serosurveillance among Canadian blood donors in four regions, replaying the series with each week’s specimens subsampled to the selected design. In simulations, the policy increased sampling effort during an anticipated high-variance period, and the share of intervals meeting the width target (0.970) agreed with validated assurance (0.974). After an unanticipated change in transmission rate, validated assurance stayed at 0.960 while the share meeting the target fell to 0.894 (95% Monte Carlo interval 0.869 to 0.919) in the transition window. Sampling effort rose while the filter relearned the transmission rate, then fell. In the case study, recommended sample sizes tracked the one-step predictive uncertainty and were largest during the Omicron wave, and the 90% filtering interval had width at most 0.10 in 94% of region-rounds with specimens. The modular framework extends to other pathogens, data streams, and surveillance objectives.

Read more

entry.title: A multi-stage probabilistic framework to estimate gas-fired generator performance during extreme winter weather

link.title: A multi-stage probabilistic framework to estimate gas-fired generator performance during extreme winter weather

entry.content:
Extreme winter weather has repeatedly disrupted gas-fired power generation in the United States, yet the plant-level data needed to systematically quantify outage risk remain proprietary. Using publicly available weather and electricity demand data together with anonymized generator contingency records from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC), we develop a three-stage Bayesian probabilistic framework for estimating winter-driven generator performance. Applied to New York State (2013–2022), the framework sequentially estimates: the hourly probability of a generator contingency event, the expected net available capacity conditioned on an event occurring, and the event duration. Colder conditions and higher electricity demand are associated with higher failure probability, lower retained capacity, and longer event duration. Under the most severe observed stress conditions, estimated mean hourly event probability reaches 24\% , while expected mean net available capacity falls to 13\% of nameplate rating. Full outage events have a median duration of 12.7 hours, while partial derating event duration increases from 2.4 to 7.1 hours with capacity loss severity. The proposed framework establishes a transferable baseline that utilities with access to plant-level records can directly extend to obtain more precise reliability estimates for operational planning and resource adequacy assessment.

Read more

entry.title: A multivariate unsupervised lognormal-GPD mixture for dependent losses

link.title: A multivariate unsupervised lognormal-GPD mixture for dependent losses

entry.content:
We propose a multivariate two-population mixture distribution for heavy-tailed and positively skewed non-negative data. The first mixture population is a multivariate lognormal, while the second is a distribution obtained by joining univariate zero-mean generalized Pareto densities via a Gumbel copula. The model is unsupervised, since no threshold has to be set or estimated. We derive some properties of the distribution and develop an Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation, which is found to perform well in multivariate contexts beyond the bivariate case. The finite-sample properties of the estimators are assessed by means of simulation experiments, and an empirical application to aggregated commercial property-casualty insurance claims illustrates the impact of dependence on risk estimation. All the methods are implemented in the R package MultLognGPD, available on Github.

Read more

entry.title: Anticipating Continued Global Fertility Decline via Neural Forecasting

link.title: Anticipating Continued Global Fertility Decline via Neural Forecasting

entry.content:
As fertility falls across much of the world, major projection systems disagree about whether decline will give way to recovery, reflecting different assumptions about post-transitional fertility. We ask instead what the historical record suggests, using NeuralTFR, a recurrent neural network that learns fertility dynamics solely from pooled histories of 230 countries and territories. In out-of-sample forecasts from three origins, it predicts fifteen years ahead as accurately as the United Nations’ Bayesian model, and its prediction intervals score slightly better. Its forecasts reveal a simple nonlinear relationship, which a spline regression reproduces with similar accuracy: fertility tends to rise slightly from the lowest levels and decline from higher ones, with recent trends affecting the size of these changes more than their direction. By 2038, these dynamics leave very low fertility, below 1.5 births per woman, more widespread than the United Nations expects, without the extreme lows of the most pessimistic projections.

Read more

entry.title: Are New Parties Shut Out of the UK House of Commons?

link.title: Are New Parties Shut Out of the UK House of Commons?

entry.content:
In recent years it has been claimed that new political parties are shut out of the UK House of Commons because they are rarely elected. At the same time, general political understanding seems to be that the House of Commons is currently further away from a pure two-party distribution of seats than at any time in the past century, perhaps longer. Although this might seem like a paradox it is possible for both of these things to have credence. We present an analysis that shows that the number of new political parties elected to the House of Commons has been slowly declining over the last century. We illustrate this both by regression and Good-Turing analyses. We also analyse the lifetime and persistence of political parties as well as present metrics that indicate the recent increased political diversity and identify the nadir of diversity in the mid-1960s and early 1970s.

Read more

entry.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Development: Building Rigorous, Decision-Ready Evidence

link.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Development: Building Rigorous, Decision-Ready Evidence

entry.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping the pharmaceutical lifecycle, from discovery and clinical development through manufacturing and regulatory review to safety surveillance and health economics, creating evidentiary challenges that predictive performance alone cannot address. This review examines the inferential, causal, validation, and documentation requirements for AI-enabled evidence generation in high-stakes settings and argues that they must be built into workflows. We outline the evidentiary functions that AI-derived outputs must satisfy before supporting consequential decisions: estimand definition, fit-for-purpose data collection, bias control, uncertainty quantification, validation, interpretability, and decision-grade documentation. Because AI both depends on and accelerates large-scale, non-randomized data collection, the integration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with real-world data (RWD) is where its evidentiary risks concentrate; we therefore present a five-step causal roadmap for that integration, in which external data supplement but never replace a concurrent control, and characterize the safeguards required across development, pharmacovigilance, regulation, and health technology assessment. Priority frontiers answer recurring implementation problems: conformal prediction for overconfident predictions, randomization-based inference for scarce data, and federated causal inference and privacy-preserving generative modeling for data that cannot be pooled. Evidence generation depends not on competition between RCTs and RWD, or between statistics and AI/ML, but on their principled synthesis under causal and inferential frameworks, with statistical expertise central to decision-ready evidence.

Read more

entry.title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning

link.title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning

entry.content:
Offline reinforcement learning is fundamentally limited by the coverage of the available data, while collecting additional trajectories through online exploration may be costly, unsafe, or infeasible. We study whether this limitation can be overcome without directly interacting with the underlying environment. Motivated by practical settings such as collaborator-mediated simulation, where a collaborator can provide information complementary to the offline data, we introduce query-based collaborative reinforcement learning to study how to acquire this information efficiently. The learner starts with a fixed offline dataset and adaptively queries state-time pairs; the collaborator samples an action according to a fixed, possibly suboptimal policy, and the simulator returns the corresponding reward and next state. For finite-horizon tabular problems, we derive an instance-dependent information-theoretic lower bound on the additional queries required to identify an $\epsilon$-optimal policy and develop a local quadratic approximation. Guided by this characterization, we develop an adaptive query-allocation algorithm whose query complexity nearly matches the local benchmark under suitable conditions. Experiments on multiple synthetic and semi-synthetic environments demonstrate the empirical efficiency of the proposed method.

Read more

entry.title: Attention-Based Multiple Instance Regression for Remote Sensing

link.title: Attention-Based Multiple Instance Regression for Remote Sensing

entry.content:
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to tackle the multiple instance regression (MIR) problem. This problem arises when the data is a collection of bags, where each bag is made of multiple instances corresponding to the same unique real-valued label. Our goal is to train a regression model which maps the instances of an unseen bag to its unique label. This MIR setting is common to remote sensing applications where there is high variability in the measurements and low geographical variability in the quantity being estimated. Our approach, in contrast to most competing methods, does not make the assumption that there exists a prime instance responsible for the label in each bag. Instead, we treat each bag as a set (i.e, an unordered sequence) of instances and learn to map each bag to its unique label by using all the instances in each bag. This is done by implementing an order-invariant operation characterized by a particular type of attention mechanism. This method is very flexible as it does not require domain knowledge nor does it make any assumptions about the distribution of the instances within each bag. We test our algorithm on five real world datasets and outperform previous state-of-the-art on three of the datasets. In addition, we augment our feature space by adding the moments of each feature for each bag, as extra features, and show that while the first moments lead to higher accuracy, there is a diminishing return.

Read more

entry.title: A unified approach to outlier identification for mixed-type data

link.title: A unified approach to outlier identification for mixed-type data

entry.content:
We present an outlier identification method for mixed type data sets comprising continuous and ordinal variables. We define outliers based on using a multivariate Gaussian distribution as reference distribution for non-outliers, with a latent Gaussian assumed for ordinal variables. The proposed algorithm is based on the robust Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator for estimating the parameters of the multivariate Gaussian for the non-outliers. This is extended to account for the fact that the full Gaussian information underlying the ordinal variables is not observed. A breakdown theorem shows that replacing observations will noty stop extreme enough outliers from being identified. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated via simulations on synthetic data with various types of contamination, achieving high detection and low false positive rates. Practical relevance is illustrated through an application to Airbnb listing data containing both continuous and ordinal attributes.

Read more

entry.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects

link.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects

entry.content:
Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator and change the structural equations, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint and then evaluate the unchanged structural equations on that state. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.

Read more

entry.title: Bagel: A Fast Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection Algorithm for Linear Models via Posterior Merging

link.title: Bagel: A Fast Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection Algorithm for Linear Models via Posterior Merging

entry.content:
Bayesian online changepoint detection provides a natural framework for quantifying uncertainty about whether and when a change has occurred. It also enables the use of prior information which can increase detection power. Exact Bayesian inference sequentially updates the posterior of whether and when a change has occurred. We present a unified approach to calculating and updating this posterior for a class of regression models covering standard changepoint scenarios, such as changes in mean and slope, whilst also allowing common structure such as seasonal effects. However, naive implementation has a computational cost that increases linearly over time. We, further, introduce approximate updates that keep this cost constant. These are based on novel ideas of merging changepoint times, and are an alternative to existing pruning approaches. We show that merging enables better approximations of the posterior of when a change occurs. Furthermore, we introduce a novel condition for merging that accounts for both the posterior probability of the changepoint times and the similarity of their corresponding post-change parameters. We show that this is more accurate than conditions that only consider the former. We demonstrate the advantage of our approach on simulated data, and the Azure LLM inference traces.

entry.title: Bayesian Multiple Imputation for Functional Data

link.title: Bayesian Multiple Imputation for Functional Data

entry.content:
Missing data are pervasive in modern functional datasets, where trajectories are often sparsely or irregularly observed. Although Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) is widely used to reconstruct incomplete curves, existing approaches typically employ single imputation, leading to overly optimistic inferences in downstream analyses. To address these challenges, we develop a novel Bayesian multiple imputation framework for functional data (BAMIFun). For single-level functional data, we impose a Bayesian low-rank model that incorporates penalized spline representations to enforce smoothness of the functional domain and derive an efficient Gibbs sampler algorithm for posterior computation. In addition, we demonstrate and validate how to properly account for estimation uncertainties in downstream analysis. Furthermore, we extend the framework to multiway functional data using Functional Tensor Singular Value Decomposition (FTSVD) model, enabling Bayesian multiple imputation in settings not supported by existing methods. Simulation studies show that BAMIFun achieves substantially improved coverage and more reliable downstream inference compared to existing methods, while maintaining similar imputation accuracy. Case studies using a physical activity dataset and an infant gut microbiome dataset further demonstrate the practical advantages of our proposed methods under severe missingness. The code is available at https://github.com/ZirenJiang/BAMIFun.

Read more

entry.title: Bayesian Reconciliation of Overlapping Multi Step Forecasts: A Post Processing Framework for Cross Origin Coherence

link.title: Bayesian Reconciliation of Overlapping Multi Step Forecasts: A Post Processing Framework for Cross Origin Coherence

entry.content:
Overlapping multi step forecasts often disagree, a form of vertical instability that we term cross origin incoherence. We propose a Bayesian reconciliation framework that treats overlapping forecasts as noisy, biased measurements of a common latent trajectory. Operating as a model agnostic post processing layer, it requires no access to model internals. Simulations demonstrate substantial incoherence reduction and robust latent trajectory recovery, remaining highly resilient (correlation 0.972) even under severe nonlinear stress tests. An empirical application to S&P 500 volatility evaluates AR(1), ETS, and LSTM models. The framework reduces incoherence by over 97% across all models while delivering fully calibrated probabilistic forecasts (93% to 94% coverage). Notably, it improves point accuracy for ETS and LSTM. Furthermore, the estimated horizon specific parameters act as a diagnostic X-ray, revealing hidden biases in neural networks without requiring access to their architecture

Read more

entry.title: Benchmark Prediction with Sparse and Unpaired Cached Responses

link.title: Benchmark Prediction with Sparse and Unpaired Cached Responses

entry.content:
Evaluating a generative model on all queries from all available benchmark tasks is prohibitively expensive. As such, models are often evaluated on different subsets of tasks and/or different subsets of queries from a given task. The resulting collection of responses and the corresponding (model, task) score matrix are sparse and unpaired. In this paper, we introduce the Product Kernel Perspective Space (PKPS), a collection of low-dimensional representations of models based on their embedded responses. PKPS generalizes existing methods for representing black-box generative models by comparing responses to similar – rather than just identical – queries and is therefore able to utilize sparse and unpaired information. Theoretically, we show that benchmark prediction using PKPS is query-efficient relative to methods that only use information from dense and paired portions of the evaluation data. Empirically, we show that PKPS-based methods outperform baselines on benchmark prediction across two large benchmark suites.

Read more

entry.title: Beyond Imputation: Mask-Adaptive Conformal Prediction via Tree Embeddings on General Missing Data Mechanisms

link.title: Beyond Imputation: Mask-Adaptive Conformal Prediction via Tree Embeddings on General Missing Data Mechanisms

entry.content:
Conformal prediction (CP) provides a distribution-free framework for uncertainty quantification with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. Yet, missing values introduce distributional heterogeneity, where marginal coverage can hide systematic undercoverage for certain missingness patterns. At the same time, existing methods based on distances or smoothness require a continuous representation of partially observed covariates. Although imputation restores continuity, it obscures the missingness patterns and introduces task-dependent overhead. We develop a new CP framework that is \emph{adaptive to missingness patterns}, without imputing covariates. We rely on data augmentation by feature embedding that accounts for missingness. Our framework represents each input with missing values by a tree embedding together with its raw missingness mask, and then learns a regularized quantile score function. Varying the choices for the penalty function and the augmentation enables us to characterize three practically relevant validity levels: exact coordinate-wise validity, exact validity on observed masks, and approximate missingness-conditional guarantees for general mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR). Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support these guarantees and show that the proposed method reduces miscoverage risk while maintaining informative intervals, especially in non-MCAR settings. These results highlight the practical value of uncertainty quantification that adapts to missingness.

entry.title: Beyond least-favorable distribution pairs: asymptotically instance-optimal robust hypothesis testing

link.title: Beyond least-favorable distribution pairs: asymptotically instance-optimal robust hypothesis testing

entry.content:
When testing a composite null $\mathcal{P}$ against a composite alternative $\mathcal{Q}$, it has been known since Huber and Strassen (1973) that if a least favorable distribution (LFD) pair exists, then a version of its likelihood ratio yields a minimax optimal test, and Huber (1965) derived a similar result in the sequential setting for a specific robust testing problem that is the focus of the current paper; the same likelihood ratio is log-optimal in the worst case; its expected logarithm under the alternative equals $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P},S \in \mathcal{Q}} KL(S|P)$, whose inverse also determines the stopping time of the test under the alternative. These results focus on optimizing worst-case performance, but the resulting methods have lower power if the data come from simpler alternatives. This paper studies an arguably more practical goal of achieving asymptotic \emph{instance optimality} for ``power-one’’ sequential tests, which remarkably may even be possible when $\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{P}^c$. This means that when the data are drawn from any $S \in \mathcal{P}^c$, the test has power one, and its stopping time is determined by the larger information number $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}} KL(S|P)$, which governs the performance of an oracle that knows $S$. To demonstrate this point, our paper focuses on the case of testing a TV ball around a discrete distribution with $d$ components, and designs a computationally and memory efficient algorithm that is also asymptotically instance-optimal. Specifically, we consider two different asymptotic settings: one is the “Wald setting”, where the type-1 error level $\alpha$ approaches zero for a fixed alternative $S$ and the second is the “Farrell setting”, where $\alpha$ is fixed and $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}} KL(S|P)$ approaches $0$. Our sequential test is simultaneously optimal in both regimes.

Read more

entry.title: Bootstrap Inference for Riemannian Optimization Problems

link.title: Bootstrap Inference for Riemannian Optimization Problems

entry.content:
We develop an online multiplier bootstrap for manifold-valued parameters estimated by averaging the iterates of Riemannian stochastic approximation. The method runs weighted iterations alongside the original algorithm, with each path using the same observations while updating its own state and intrinsic average. The weighted averages provide uncertainty assessments without a plug-in asymptotic covariance estimator. Under local stability and regularity conditions, we establish bootstrap consistency and show that a fixed number of paths suffices for asymptotically valid Student intervals and intrinsic confidence regions. The theory accommodates samplewise nonsmooth scores and identifies a critical oracle-bias regime in which the estimator’s limiting distribution shifts, but the centered bootstrap distribution does not. Applications include spherical means, positive-definite matrix means and medians, and principal-subspace estimation. Simulations show coverage close to nominal in regular settings, and an analysis of North Atlantic storm locations illustrates descriptive online inference for a spherical center.

Read more

entry.title: Causal DAG-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Physical Activity Maintenance: Using Prior Data to Inform Future Deployment

link.title: Causal DAG-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Physical Activity Maintenance: Using Prior Data to Inform Future Deployment

entry.content:
Digital health interventions can provide scalable, personalized support for physical activity (PA), yet sustaining PA over the long-term remains difficult. Because affective experiences with PA are important for activity sustainment, we developed an online reinforcement learning (RL) system for the forthcoming ADAPT factorial trial that personalizes twice-daily activity suggestions aimed at improving affective associations with PA. This setting poses several challenges: participant-specific data are scarce relative to the candidate state space, important states and rewards are partially observed, interventions are frequent while the primary outcome is measured weekly, and activity suggestions can both improve PA-related experiences and increase intervention burden. We address these challenges using an expert-specified causal directed acyclic graph as an integrated RL design tool, guiding state construction, estimation of partially observed states, delayed credit assignment, and representation of beneficial and adverse intervention pathways. We further construct a longitudinal simulator calibrated from a prior micro-randomized trial to compare candidate RL designs under realistic state evolution, missingness, and participant heterogeneity before deployment. Together, this work illustrates how causal domain knowledge and prior trial data can make long-horizon, participant-specific RL more practical for digital health interventions targeting sustained behavior change.

Read more

entry.title: Causal Inference and Evidence Synthesis for Semi-continuous Exposures with Multiple Outcomes

link.title: Causal Inference and Evidence Synthesis for Semi-continuous Exposures with Multiple Outcomes

entry.content:
Semi-continuous exposure variables, featuring a point mass at zero and a continuous dose in exposed individuals, arise frequently in epidemiology. In such settings, investigators may wish to distinguish the causal effect of exposure at a fixed dose with no exposure, from the dose-response effect among exposed individuals. We develop a two-stage framework for causal inference with semi-continuous exposures and multiple outcomes. The proposed approach yields outcome-specific estimators for these two causal components, establishes their large sample properties, and provides Wald-type tests for homogeneity across outcomes. We further extend the framework to the multi-cohort setting through hierarchical homogeneity testing and evidence synthesis, enabling principled pooling across cohorts and outcomes. We apply the proposed methods to several cohort studies designed to evaluate the effects of prenatal alcohol exposure on executive function, mathematics achievement, and learning and memory. Simulation studies show that the proposed estimators and testing procedures perform well. The framework provides a principled basis for estimation, comparison, and synthesis of causal effects with multiple outcomes and semi-continuous exposures.

Read more

entry.title: Causal Inference from Self-controlled Case Series

link.title: Causal Inference from Self-controlled Case Series

entry.content:
The self-controlled case series (SCCS) design is widely used in studies of rare events, for example of vaccine side effects. Conceptually, the design has two main features. First, it requires only data from individuals who have experienced the event of interest. Therefore, the design is especially useful when the outcome is rare and the available data come from surveillance or clinical records, say, of hospitalized patients. Second, because comparisons are made within single individuals, time-invariant confounding between treatment and outcome is eliminated. We formulate a set of sufficient identification assumptions for estimating the causal effect of vaccination on an adverse outcome under the SCCS design, drawing on ideas from the causal inference literature. Unlike the existing SCCS literature, we do not consider a parametric model as the starting point. This allows us to establish when and why the SCCS design allows identification of causal effects, using data from cases only. However, because the sufficient identifiability assumptions are implausible in some applications, we also develop statistical tests for the existence of a treatment effect that remain valid when only a subset of the identification assumptions holds.

Read more

entry.title: Causal Mediation Analysis with High-Dimensional Surrogates: Identification, Estimation and Inference under Latent Factor Models

link.title: Causal Mediation Analysis with High-Dimensional Surrogates: Identification, Estimation and Inference under Latent Factor Models

entry.content:
Causal mediation analysis is an important tool for understanding how a treatment affects an outcome through intermediate variables referred to as mediators. However, in many applications, these mediators and pre-treatment covariates are not directly observed and are instead measured through noisy, high-dimensional surrogates. Mediation analysis when such latent variables are observed only through these surrogates remains less explored. In this paper, we propose Factor-Adjusted Regression for Mediation Analysis (FARMA), a factor-based framework for estimating direct and indirect effects when either one or both of the mediators and relevant pre-treatment covariates are latent. FARMA uses the surrogate measurements to recover information about the underlying latent variables. Under a latent factor structure, we show that the direct and indirect effects are approximately identified, with an approximation error that vanishes as the surrogate dimensions grow. We further show that our estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal. We combine the theory with extensive simulation studies and apply it to data from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) study, where we investigate whether the effect of depressive symptoms on cognitive impairment is mediated through the latent process underlying high-dimensional DNA methylation measurements.

entry.title: Causal Record Linkage

link.title: Causal Record Linkage

entry.content:
Combining observations from multiple data sources creates a valuable resource for research. In causal inference, record linkage methods grant researchers access to the covariates needed for unbiased estimation and offer the means to explore (long-term) outcomes. This paper examines how record linkage conflicts with the assumptions required for identifying causal effects. Our investigation reveals that linkage errors primarily threaten consistency in the causal framework, leading to attenuation bias in the inference due to discrepancies in the linked data. In attempting to address this bias by being more stringent on the linkage, sampling bias inadvertently emerges from a covariate shift between the baseline and the linked samples, as profiles with more distinctive information are more likely to be recovered. Despite these challenges, we identify settings in which record linkage and causal inference can be soundly combined, and show how the effect estimated on linked data can be generalised, with linkage decisions informed accordingly. We further identify when existing and novel solutions support valid causal inference on linked data, and when inference should instead be treated with caution or even abandoned. We illustrate the challenges raised and the potential solutions using real data from a study of women’s health and a simulation study.

Read more

entry.title: Causal discovery needs explicit epistemic standards

link.title: Causal discovery needs explicit epistemic standards

entry.content:
There are many causal discovery algorithms, but few guiding principles for choosing between them. Methods are usually compared through three lenses: identifiability, consistency, and benchmarks. Each introduces assumptions about the data-generating process that are often untestable. We argue that there are no shared standards for comparing, prioritizing, or even discussing those assumptions. We support this claim by showing that (i) identifiability assumptions are often preferred by convention rather than by principle, (ii) uniform consistency requires further untestable assumptions, while the weaker pointwise consistency has arguably narrowed algorithm design, and (iii) benchmarks are not neutral tests but carry an epistemic role of their own: they quietly fix which regimes matter, which guarantees come into play, and what counts as success. In doing so, they shape what algorithm comparisons are taken to show and thus perform some of the same epistemic work as theory, but less transparently. In this position paper we argue for a more transparent, integrated practice: Make the epistemic standards for discussing identifiability and consistency assumptions explicit, especially their failure modes and scope conditions; design benchmarks to operationalize those standards, by stress-testing and ablating both. Then, theoretical and empirical results jointly clarify when, why, and how algorithms may work rather than accumulate as disconnected advances.

Read more

entry.title: Certified computation of Buehler confidence limits for system reliability

link.title: Certified computation of Buehler confidence limits for system reliability

entry.content:
Component tests can support a lower confidence limit for a system that has not been tested as a whole, but numerical optimization can compromise its coverage. A feasible point in the minimization defining a Buehler limit gives an upper bound on that limit; reporting it can therefore overstate reliability. We develop a computation that maintains lower and upper bounds on the ideal endpoint for a prescribed ordering. Bounds over entire parameter regions justify the reported lower endpoint at every completed checkpoint, including under adaptive stopping and selection among runs. Separate refinement conditions establish convergence, and an explicit error allocation accounts for simulated tail probabilities and confidence-region localization. The theory retains nuisance and dependence parameters in the observation model. Monotone corner bounds give the implemented specialization for scalar and two-component binomial systems; Bernstein and probability-distance bounds provide further theoretical constructions. Four benchmark problems reach a certified width of $10^{-5}$ under each of four search strategies. Additional stochastic candidates increase cost without reducing subdivisions, whereas complete sample-space enumeration verifies the implemented coverage at three parameter vectors. For the all-success example, the certified lower limit is $0.68128$, compared with $0.41738$ from Bonferroni-adjusted component limits.

Read more

Four benchmark problems reach a certified width of $10^{-5}$ under each of four search strategies. Additional stochastic candidates increase cost without reducing subdivisions, whereas complete sample-space enumeration verifies the implemented coverage at three parameter vectors. For the all-success example, the certified lower limit is $0.68128$, compared with $0.41738$ from Bonferroni-adjusted component limits.

entry.title: Certifying Residual Architectures from Their Primitives: Growth Exponents and Criticality

link.title: Certifying Residual Architectures from Their Primitives: Growth Exponents and Criticality

entry.content:
Whether a deep residual architecture avoids numerical blow-up in its forward and backward dynamics is typically determined through costly trial-and-error training. Existing stabilization strategies, including normalization and residual scaling, lack a common framework for predicting their effects across architectures. We develop an a priori certification framework based on two exponents derived from architectural primitives: the forward growth exponent $q$ and the Jacobian sensitivity exponent $\sigma$. These exponents characterize stability regimes and determine how certified allowable depth scales with the floating-point limit $M$. In particular, $q=1$ marks a sharp threshold: for $\sigma>0$, certified depth scales as $\log M/\log\log M$, $\sqrt{\log M}$, and $\log_q\log M$ in the regimes $q<1$, $q=1$, and $q>1$, respectively, exhibiting changes reminiscent of phase transitions in statistical physics. The sensitivity exponent $\sigma$ further constrains backward stability, even when $q\le1$. Exponent arithmetic enables certification from computation graphs, including heterogeneous residual stacks, and identifies targeted modifications to existing backbones without uniform normalization. Experiments on Mamba, PatchTST, FNO, GPT-2, and a Toto~2.0 proxy support the predicted stability distinctions: controlling superlinear growth prevents divergence in Mamba and Toto~2.0, while reducing attention sensitivity restores stable GPT-2 training. Among stable designs, $q=1$ architectures can outperform normalized $q=0$ counterparts in forecasting and operator-learning extrapolation. Rather than prescribing a single architecture, our framework identifies families of architectures with certifiable stability, narrowing the scope of trial-and-error and enabling systematic, task-dependent exploration before training.

entry.title: Characterizing Estimator-Regime Transitions in Adaptive Enrichment Trials

link.title: Characterizing Estimator-Regime Transitions in Adaptive Enrichment Trials

entry.content:
Adaptive enrichment trials that identify responsive subpopulations allocate a fixed sample across them and estimate each one’s effect from the resulting data. For a synthetic control design with adaptive recruitment and borrowing of control outcomes, we ask whether a doubly robust family of targeted maximum likelihood estimators should replace its sample mean; the choice can be made largely at the design stage. A crossing condition weighs the bias removed and the efficiency gained by the doubly robust family against the finite-sample inflation of nuisance estimation; an equal-error boundary, located by simulation, separates the families in the plane of sample size and bias. A consistency principle prices recruiting with the wrong family’s variance functional. With three and eight simulated subpopulations the boundary’s sign prediction for the mean squared error difference holds in $99.6\%$ of $10{,}302$ comparisons decided at two standard errors. A pre-specified selector commits to the doubly robust family where the squared anticipated bias exceeds the net variance term. Recruiting along that family’s path costs up to $0.035$ in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; recruiting with the sample mean functional and routing only the analysis removes this cost and about nine tenths of its error excess.

Read more

entry.title: Clapping: Removing Per-sample Storage for Pipeline Parallel Distributed Optimization with Communication Compression

link.title: Clapping: Removing Per-sample Storage for Pipeline Parallel Distributed Optimization with Communication Compression

entry.content:
Pipeline-parallel distributed optimization is essential for large-scale machine learning but is challenged by significant communication overhead from transmitting high-dimensional activations and gradients between workers. Existing approaches often depend on impractical unbiased gradient assumptions or incur sample-size memory overhead. This paper introduces Clapping, a Communication compression algorithm with LAzy samPling for Pipeline-parallel learnING. Clapping adopts a lazy sampling strategy that reuses data samples across steps, breaking sample-wise memory barrier and supporting convergence in few-epoch or online regimes. Clapping comprises two variants including Clapping-FC and Clapping-FU, both of which achieve convergence without unbiased assumption for compressed gradient, effectively addressing compression error propagation in multi-worker settings. Numerical experiments validate the performance of Clapping across different tasks.

Read more

entry.title: Clustering extremal dependence structures via Wasserstein distances between angular measures

link.title: Clustering extremal dependence structures via Wasserstein distances between angular measures

entry.content:
Grouping random vectors by their joint extremal behaviour is a recurring task in climate science, hydrology, and finance. Classical clustering is driven by typical observations, while existing extremal procedures either summarize dependence by a single coefficient or discretize the simplex in an ad hoc way. We propose a dissimilarity that compares complete angular measures by optimal transport: each angular measure is estimated above a high radial threshold, mapped from the simplex into a Euclidean space of Aitchison coordinates, and compared by the 1-Wasserstein distance. The methodology is fully nonparametric and requires no fitted model. The dissimilarities feed any distance-based clustering algorithm. Under intermediate-threshold asymptotics and mild moment and separation conditions, hierarchical clustering and partitioning around medoids based on them recovers the latent partition with probability tending to one. In simulations, the proposed approach matches established competitors when clusters differ mainly in the strength of extremal dependence and performs substantially better when equal-strength clusters differ in the shape of their angular measures, especially when asymmetry drives the separation. Applications to rain–snowmelt–runoff extremes in Swiss catchments and to extremal co-movement between international equity markets and the US market reveal hydrologically and economically interpretable groups.

Read more

entry.title: Common random number simulation as the optimal coordinatewise coupling for iterated random functions

link.title: Common random number simulation as the optimal coordinatewise coupling for iterated random functions

entry.content:
In this paper, we extend the results of Glasserman and Yao (1992) to demonstrate that common random number (CRN) simulation applied to coordinatewise monotone iterated random functions (IRF) represents the optimal allocation of random numbers to minimize the expected distance of an $n$-step Markov chain (MC) in $\mathbb{R}^q$. We introduce this concept as the optimal coordinatewise Wasserstein distance (CWD) coupling. We provide specific examples of IRFs where CRN is the optimal CWD coupling, as well as cases where it is not. For IRFs that are not coordinatewise monotone, we illustrate how CRN applied to equimeasurable transformations can result in even lower expected distances compared to CRN applied to the original IRF.

Read more

entry.title: Conditional independence testing through marginal permutation

link.title: Conditional independence testing through marginal permutation

entry.content:
Marginal permutation is exact for testing marginal independence but generally invalid for conditional independence because it breaks the dependence between the exposure ($\bm X$) and covariates ($\bm Z$). In this paper, we show that empirical studentization can nevertheless make this deliberately misspecified resampling scheme asymptotically valid for important conditional independence tests based on scores. The resulting procedures are novel in the sense that they are valid in finite samples when the exposure is marginally independent of the outcome ($\bm Y$) and covariates, and asymptotically valid under the broader conditional independence null, $\bm X\indep \bm Y\mid \bm Z$, subject to method-specific conditions. For generalized linear model scores, separately studentizing the observed and permuted scores yields validity under a correctly specified null mean despite \emph{arbitrary} conditional variance misspecification. Moreover, the permutation calibration also applies to tests based on generalized and projected covariance measures. Their validity accommodates machine learning nuisance estimates under a condition on the stability of refitting after permutation, for which we provide sufficient conditions for common regression learners. Permutation calibration preserves first-order local power while better capturing the finite-sample discreteness and skewness induced by sparse observations. Simulations and single-cell CRISPR screen analysis show substantial calibration gains with our methods when effective sample size is small.

Read more

entry.title: Conditioning Gaussian Processes on Almost Anything

link.title: Conditioning Gaussian Processes on Almost Anything

entry.content:
Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled probabilistic model over functions, but exact inference is restricted to the linear-Gaussian regime. We establish an explicit equivalence between GPs and a class of linear diffusion models, recasting predictive sampling as an ODE with closed-form Gaussian dynamics and a likelihood-dependent guidance term that admits a simple Monte Carlo approximation. In the linear-Gaussian setting, we recover standard GP conditioning exactly; beyond conjugacy, the same machinery handles any conditioning statement admitting point-wise likelihood evaluation - including non-linear physics, and, for the first time, natural language via large language models. Whitening isolates the irreducible non-Gaussian dynamics, minimising Wasserstein-2 transport cost and eliminating numerical stiffness. The result is a general-purpose GP inference scheme requiring no bespoke derivations. Together, these results provide a general mechanism for incorporating the full richness of real-world knowledge as conditioning information, opening a new frontier for the probabilistic modelling of real-world problems.

Read more

entry.title: Conformal Bayes under Continuous Label Shift: Sensitivity Analysis and the Limits of Exact Validity

link.title: Conformal Bayes under Continuous Label Shift: Sensitivity Analysis and the Limits of Exact Validity

entry.content:
Conformal Bayes combines Bayesian posterior predictive scores with conformal calibration. Under continuous label shift, both the score and calibration weights depend on an unknown response density ratio. Existing methods typically estimate a single exponential tilt from pseudo-labels or predictive samples and plug it into calibration. We propose Joint Tilt-Sensitivity Conformal Bayes (JTS-CB), which performs sensitivity analysis over a prespecified family of tilts. Each tilt defines a coupled score-weight pair. The split procedure, JTS-SCB, solves joint min-max calibration by taking the largest tilt-specific threshold from weighted intercept-only quantile regression. JTS-Union retains individual thresholds, yielding prediction sets contained in those of JTS-SCB. Both use calibration-only weights by design, without a general coverage guarantee. We also study a candidate-weighted exact counterpart. Any nonzero linear exponential tilt makes its prediction set unbounded, whereas compact negative-quadratic families yield bounded exact unions under Gaussian scores. For the practical procedures, a localized correction with fallback gives coverage at least nominal minus a target tail-mass bound when the family contains the true tilt, but can substantially increase width. Experiments on controlled shifts of three regression datasets and on synthetic data show that plug-in predictive sampling can approach oracle coverage when the shift is well identified, but remains vulnerable to predictive bias and unstable tilt estimation. Sensitivity analysis can mitigate these failures in the tested settings, at the cost of wider prediction sets. Coupling scores and weights can yield narrower sets with higher coverage than varying weights alone, although this advantage is not uniform across shifts. Excluding the true tilt from the sensitivity family can still cause undercoverage.

Read more
