entry.title: Continuum-marginal optimal transport: a mesh-free kernel method

link.title: Continuum-marginal optimal transport: a mesh-free kernel method

entry.content:
In this paper we study continuum-marginal optimal transport. Given a time-continuous family of probability marginals, the problem is to recover the minimum-energy velocity field whose flow reproduces every marginal. This problem is the continuum limit of the classical two-marginal Benamou-Brenier formulation, and also the deterministic limit of the Nelson problem of stochastic optimal transport. We propose a practical mesh-free solver for this problem. The weak continuity equation is embedded in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, yielding a sample-only objective that requires no spatial discretization. The velocity is parametrized by any linear-in-parameters dictionary or neural network, and is optimized by mini-batch stochastic methods. Synthetic experiments confirm that the method achieves accurate drift recovery and marginal consistency. The same computational framework also applies to the Nelson problem.

Read more

entry.title: Convex Regression at Scale: Geometry-Preserving Constraint Sparsification

link.title: Convex Regression at Scale: Geometry-Preserving Constraint Sparsification

entry.content:
Convex regression provides a flexible nonparametric estimation framework while incorporating appropriate shape information. However, its standard least-squares formulation has $O(n^2)$ supporting-hyperplane constraints creating a computational bottleneck as the sample size $n$ increases. We study a $K$-nearest-neighbor (KNN) localized relaxation for convex regression where we for each sample, we only maintain the $K$ nearest hyperplane constraints. Under mild regularity conditions, we establish statistical guarantees for our modified estimator in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. In particular, for $d>4$, the population risk of our modified problem can be shown to have equivalent convergence rates as the original least square convex regression estimator of $\widetilde O(n^{-2/d})$ using neighborhoods sizes (i.e. $K=K_n$) of order $\widetilde O(n^{2(d-1)/(2d-1)})$ for general convex functions and $\widetilde O(n^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$ for strongly convex functions. To corroborate our theory, we implement iterative optimization methods to compare the prediction accuracy of the KNN relaxation with those of the full estimator across synthetic convex benchmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that KNN prediction risk approaches the full-estimator prediction risk at neighborhood sizes matching the theoretical scale.

Read more

entry.title: Correctness and Predictive Uncertainty in Bayesian TSK Fuzzy Regression: A Reproducible Evaluation on Tabular and Building-Meter Data

link.title: Correctness and Predictive Uncertainty in Bayesian TSK Fuzzy Regression: A Reproducible Evaluation on Tabular and Building-Meter Data

entry.content:
Uncertainty estimates from fuzzy regression are informative only when the implementation is correct and the comparison protocol makes the sources of variation visible. We revisit a first-order Takagi–Sugeno–Kang (TSK) regression implementation and rebuild its dense, conjugate Bayesian, BIC-based, and rule-level spike-and-slab estimators using corrected code. The corrected pipeline freezes the Gaussian membership partition at training time, uses a scaled conjugate prior, evaluates firing strengths in the log domain, and reports direct posterior-predictive quantiles for Bayesian methods. Across 30 outer 80/20 splits on three targets from two UCI regression datasets, corrected TSK-LS obtains $R^2=0.957$, $0.923$, and $0.786$ on Energy-Heating, Energy-Cooling, and Concrete, respectively; rule-level Gibbs sampling with Bayesian model averaging obtains $0.957$, $0.922$, and $0.784$. We then evaluate the same workflow on a bounded chronological sample of the Building Data Genome 2 meter data that covers 158 buildings across 17 sites. In a common-unit evaluation, every method is scored on the same 47,400 test rows and every trained model uses 94,800 train–validation rows. Persistence has RMSE $27.710$, compared with $29.083$ for both TSK-LS and Bayesian TSK; the pre-specified building-level mean RMSE difference between Bayesian TSK and persistence is $+0.0447$ with a 95% site-cluster bootstrap interval of $[-1.5536,1.5665]$. The Bayesian TSK 90% intervals have PICP $0.980$ and MPIW $116.469$. Taken together, the evidence supports a narrower conclusion: spike-and-slab model averaging is a reproducible implementation option, but it does not provide a demonstrated accuracy or calibration advantage across the tested tabular and building-meter settings.

entry.title: Correlation Matters! Streamlining the Sample Size Procedure with Hierarchical Time-to-event Endpoints

link.title: Correlation Matters! Streamlining the Sample Size Procedure with Hierarchical Time-to-event Endpoints

entry.content:
Composite endpoints are widely used in cardiovascular clinical trials to improve statistical efficiency while preserving clinical relevance. The win ratio (WR) measure and more general frameworks of win statistics have emerged as popular alternatives to traditional time-to-first-event analyses. Although analytic sample size formulas for WR have been developed, they rely on design parameters that are often not straightforward to specify. Consequently, sample size determination in clinical trials with WR for the primary analysis is most often based on simulations, which, however, can be computationally intensive. To address this challenge, we derive refined formulas to calculate the proportions of wins, losses, and ties for multiple prioritized time-to-event endpoints to assist with study planning. These formulas rely on familiar design inputs and become directly applicable when integrated with existing sample size methods. We conduct a comprehensive assessment of how correlation among endpoints affects sample size requirements across varying design features, and demonstrate the role of correlations through case studies to generate further insights.

Read more

entry.title: Data integration using propensity score weighting under missing at random

link.title: Data integration using propensity score weighting under missing at random

entry.content:
We study data integration for the setting in which a probability sample and a nonprobability sample are both available from a common target population, with auxiliary variables observed in both samples and the study variable observed only in the nonprobability sample. Under a parametric propensity score model for the nonprobability sample inclusion mechanism, we develop a conditional maximum likelihood estimator of the inclusion probabilities and construct an inverse probability weighted (IPW) estimator of the population mean. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed IPW estimator under suitable regularity conditions. To guard against misspecification of the propensity score model, we further incorporate an outcome regression model through debiased generalized entropy calibration (GEC) yielding a doubly robust estimator that remains consistent when the propensity score model or the outcome regression model is correctly specified. We also develop variance estimation procedures for both estimators. Simulation studies illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods, and we apply them to data from the Culture and Community in a Time of Crisis survey, where the nonprobability sample substantially over-represents certain demographic groups relative to the U.S.\ adult population.

entry.title: Decomposition Atlases of Brains and Kidneys from Postmortem CT: Shape and Topological Data Analysis

link.title: Decomposition Atlases of Brains and Kidneys from Postmortem CT: Shape and Topological Data Analysis

entry.content:
Forensic assessments of postmortem decomposition often rely on external, whole-body signs, yet structural changes within organs remain largely unquantified. Using whole-body computed tomography scans of 59 decedents from the New Mexico Decedent Image Database, we conduct an organ-level statistical shape analysis of decomposing brains and kidneys, representing each organ as a three-dimensional point cloud of its outer surface and internal cavity boundaries. Decomposition creates voids, fragmentation, and structural heterogeneity, complicating point correspondence. Registration-based principal component analysis and principal nested cones yield interpretable orderings for brains only. We therefore construct a registration-free pipeline using persistent homology and a fusion of complementary topological distances selected through simulations of cavity formation and growth. Clustering identifies broad patterns of internal decay, and seriation produces organ-specific decomposition atlases. The brain atlas combines geometric and topological rankings; the kidney atlas uses topology alone. Rank agreement is higher between paired kidneys (Kendall’s $\tau = 0.59$) than between brains and kidneys ($\tau = 0.34$ to $0.39$), indicating asynchronous decompositions within a body. Whole-body stages agree more closely with brain than with kidney rankings. These findings support quantitative forensic taphonomy by complementing whole-body staging with organ-level, interior-based measurements. We release the organ point clouds and analysis code to support research on organ decomposition and shape analysis without reliable correspondence.

entry.title: Decoupled Kemeny quasi-likelihoods for rank-based generalised linear models

link.title: Decoupled Kemeny quasi-likelihoods for rank-based generalised linear models

entry.content:
This paper introduces a unified profile quasi-likelihood framework for generalised linear models built on a topologically complete extension to Kendall’s $\tau$ with finite sample power and Type-I error rates. By establishing equivalence between continuous $L^2$ profile estimators and discrete Generalized Gibbs exponential families, we prove local asymptotic minimax efficiency over the copula tangent space. The framework yields monotone-affine invariant inference, sub-Gaussian concentration bounds, and exact finite-sample $t$-pivot tail majorization under arbitrary tie configurations. We illustrate the methodology through three canonical applications: bivariate rank correlation, paired testing, and intraclass correlation.

entry.title: Deep Bootstrap

link.title: Deep Bootstrap

entry.content:
In this work, we propose a novel deep bootstrap framework for nonparametric regression based on conditional diffusion models. Specifically, we construct a conditional diffusion model to learn the distribution of the response variable given the covariates. This model is then used to generate bootstrap samples by pairing the original covariates with newly synthesized responses. We reformulate nonparametric regression as conditional sample mean estimation, which is implemented directly via the learned conditional diffusion model. Unlike traditional bootstrap methods that decouple the estimation of the conditional distribution, sampling, and nonparametric regression, our approach integrates these components into a unified generative framework. With the expressive capacity of diffusion models, our method facilitates both efficient sampling from high-dimensional or multimodal distributions and accurate nonparametric estimation. We establish rigorous theoretical guarantees for the proposed method. In particular, we derive optimal end-to-end convergence rates in the Wasserstein distance between the learned and target conditional distributions. Building on this foundation, we further establish the convergence guarantees of the resulting bootstrap procedure. Numerical studies demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our approach for complex regression tasks.

Read more

entry.title: Deformed Q-learning for High-Dimensional Dynamic Treatment Regimes

link.title: Deformed Q-learning for High-Dimensional Dynamic Treatment Regimes

entry.content:
In high-dimensional dynamic treatment regimes, nonlinear terminal outcome models complicate upstream conditional-mean modeling and inference based on recursively estimated continuation values. We introduce a Deformed Q-learning procedure for general action spaces that accommodates a terminal-stage GLM, random designs, conditional heteroscedasticity, and fine-grained action discretization. The procedure changes the recursive criterion by propagating the terminal deformed optimal Q-function through sparse block-wise linear conditional-mean models. Under the stated models and regularity conditions, we establish consistent and asymptotically normal estimators, accounting for downstream estimation uncertainty in inference for optimal Q-values, deformed optimal Q-values, and their contrasts. We bound population regret relative to the original terminal mean-outcome objective without explicit stage-wise accumulation. Estimation and inference also extend to a growing number of stages under conditions uniform across stages. Simulation studies demonstrate accurate estimation and variable selection. In an empirical application to sepsis management using the MIMIC-III database, the proposed framework supports stage-specific value inference, while an auxiliary action-alignment analysis provides an exploratory signal that early-stage concordance with the learned recommendation may be associated with improved survival.

Read more

entry.title: Dense Structural Compression of Transformers via Gauge-Correct Channel Removal

link.title: Dense Structural Compression of Transformers via Gauge-Correct Channel Removal

entry.content:
Inference energy per token drives the cost and carbon footprint of deployed transformers. It is dominated by dense matrix products that incur fused multiply-accumulate (FMA) operations and memory traffic. To reduce these computations while retaining dense tensors for high GPU throughput, we develop a methodology from first principles to adapt structural complexity during training to maximize inference utility per unit compute. Channel penalties drive entire tensor slices to zero to enable physical removal while preserving density and the network function. The natural approach, penalizing the norm of operator components acting through each channel, is provably destabilized by gauge freedom. We resolve this pathology with GaugeLasso: additive symmetric group-lasso penalties that recover a monotone function of product-norms when the network converges to gauge balance. Our equilibrium analysis enables per-channel calibration to correctly suppress slices that under-perform in inference utility per unit compute. Under adaptive pressure, the network reorganizes into depth-dependent structural profiles that can be far smaller than the architecture required to learn the task. On polynomial long division over $\mathbb{F}_{31}$, compute compresses from 148 to 255 times with perfect accuracy. On character-level language modeling, compressed models outperform the hand-designed baseline at equal FMA. On masked autoencoding, a compression trial exposes which axes were over-provisioned and which saturated, guiding a better second design. Compaction also accelerates training monotonically as the model progresses. Post-hoc pruning with the same utility ranking cannot reach these structures, showing that sustained pressure is central to discovery of efficient models. Retraining a discovered architecture recovers baseline quality on our statistical tasks, but fails on our exact algorithmic task.

entry.title: Diagnosing Model–Item Interactions in Language Model Benchmarks with LSIRM

link.title: Diagnosing Model–Item Interactions in Language Model Benchmarks with LSIRM

entry.content:
Language models with similar benchmark accuracy can succeed on different items. Overall scores do not show where their performance differs or which item properties might explain those differences. We demonstrate how the latent space item response model (LSIRM) can help evaluators investigate these patterns and their consequences for model comparison. We analyze 1,348 language models on 5,761 BBH items and compare ways of presenting and scoring answers across BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and MuSR. We examine LSIRM maps, which summarize differences in performance across models and items, alongside item properties and records of correct and incorrect responses. In BBH, nearby items on these maps often share the same correct answer, such as “Yes” or “No.” Across the four benchmarks, this pattern is stronger when answers are scored using option labels, such as A, B, C, and D, than when using the text of the options. We then estimate each model’s tendency to perform better or worse on items with particular correct answers and quantify how this tendency contributes to its score. This separates an estimated contribution associated with correct answers from the remaining differences in item performance. Two models’ total numbers of correct answers differed by only 14 out of 5,761 items. Excluding the estimated answer-category contribution from their scores moved their ranks hundreds of places in opposite directions, while keeping all other estimates unchanged. The approach helps evaluators identify differences hidden by overall accuracy and understand how the choice of what to include in a score affects model rankings.

entry.title: Diagonal Equivalence in State Space Models: Characterization, Retrieval Rank, and Selective Extensions

link.title: Diagonal Equivalence in State Space Models: Characterization, Retrieval Rank, and Selective Extensions

entry.content:
We classify real and complex state-space models (SSMs) with linear transitions, distinguishing fixed-basis diagonal equivalence from input-output equivalence and tracking coefficient-conditioning windows under coordinate changes. We characterize diagonal equivalence through commuting transition families whose members are diagonalizable over the chosen field. With time-shared token-local matrix maps, we identify this class’s state-mediated kernels with unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks. Mamba 3’s multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) construction lifts one value per local interface; SSD-MIMO routes independent values for local retrieval rank above one. HybridMamba combines Mamba 1’s per-coordinate decay, Mamba 2-style heads and Mamba 3’s complex rotations and two-endpoint writes, mixing real and rotating state blocks with different decay laws. They recover Mamba 1-3 single-input, single-output (SISO) configurations as exact special cases. On five large H100 bfloat16 workloads, our fused GPU kernels improve geometric-mean training time over official Mamba 1/3 in matched SISO recoveries, with Mamba 2 near parity at SSM-core scope. Memory tradeoffs depend on the baseline and metric: saved-for-backward versus peak allocation. In small-model multi-token recall experiments, both designs outperform Mamba 1-3 on the hardest tier; higher routing ranks perform best in gated or phase-diverse configurations. In single-seed language models with about 500M parameters, both improve on Mamba 1/2 in test loss at 2B tokens, but the routing gains do not translate into lower language-model loss. Our best configurations approach Mamba 3 SISO through 10B tokens while remaining behind it and Mamba 3 MIMO in language-model loss.

entry.title: Differential Dynamic Causal Nets: Model Construction, Identification and Group Comparisons

link.title: Differential Dynamic Causal Nets: Model Construction, Identification and Group Comparisons

entry.content:
Pathophysiological modelling of brain systems from microscale to macroscale remains difficult in group comparisons partly because of the infeasibility of modelling the interactions of thousands of neurons at the scales involved. Here, to address the challenge, we present a novel approach to construct differential causal networks directly from grouped electroencephalogram (EEG) data. In the proposed modular network, each node represents a locally averaged regional neural system via a canonical Jansen-Rit model while directed edges stand for node-wise input-output connections. The network is hierarchically structured in the sense that node and edge parameters are random, varying in subjects, but follow a mixed-effects model. We show that unlike the classical Jansen-Rit models, the proposed node models are locally structurally identifiable. An evolutionary optimisation algorithm for parameter inference in the proposed method is developed using a loss function derived from Chen-Fliess expansions of stochastic differential equations. The method is demonstrated by fitting the proposed modular network to grouped epileptic EEG data in both sensor- and source- levels. We identify significant changes in the parameters that characterise dynamic networks within and between brain regions. We reveal network disruptions, due to imbalance of excitatory-inhibitory interneurons and other altered epileptic brain connectivities, before and during seizure periods, and contrast them between case and control groups. The performance of the proposed method is also evaluated on synthetic data.

Read more

entry.title: Differential Privacy for Generalized Entropy Indices of Income Inequality

link.title: Differential Privacy for Generalized Entropy Indices of Income Inequality

entry.content:
The mean log deviation and the Theil index are two widely used measures of income inequality. The organization releasing these measures may be obligated to protect the confidentiality of the individual incomes used in the computations. In particular, the organization may wish to release versions of these measures with formal guarantees of privacy. The organization could do so by satisfying differential privacy; however, typical applications of differentially private algorithms are likely to add so much noise to the measures that they become unusable. We present differentially private algorithms for these indices with reasonable error properties. The algorithms rely on computing or approximating bounds on the smooth sensitivity, that is, the maximum absolute amount the inequality measures change when replacing any subset of the $n$ incomes in the reported data with arbitrarily chosen feasible values. For the mean log deviation, the algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time. For the Theil index, the algorithm runs in $O(n\log n)$ time. We illustrate the performance of each differentially private algorithm using individual-level and household-level income data from the Current Population Survey. We also examine repeated sampling properties of the algorithms using artificially generated data. The empirical results indicate when these differentially private algorithms can be expected to provide accurate estimates and when they are likely to introduce too much noise.

Read more

entry.title: Differentially Private Confidence Intervals for Relative Risk and Odds Ratio

link.title: Differentially Private Confidence Intervals for Relative Risk and Odds Ratio

entry.content:
Ratio statistics, such as relative risk and odds ratio, are central tools for comparing outcome probabilities across populations, particularly in clinical and epidemiological studies. However, when the underlying counts are released under differential privacy, the resulting ratio estimators can exhibit nontrivial bias and variance, and principled methods for statistical inference in this setting remain limited. In this work, we study estimation and inference for ratio statistics computed from counts perturbed by additive Laplace or Gaussian noise. We show that the natural plug-in estimators based on privatized counts are consistent, and we derive confidence intervals that explicitly account for both sampling variability and privacy-induced noise, making our approach appealing for moderate sample sizes. Our analysis provides transparent variance decompositions that clarify when privacy meaningfully affects inference. Empirical results on simulated and real datasets demonstrate that, for moderate privacy levels and sample sizes, the proposed confidence intervals closely match their non-private counterparts, while properly reflecting additional uncertainty in small-sample regimes. Our results provide both theoretical guarantees and practical guidance for conducting statistical inference with ratio statistics under differential privacy.

entry.title: Direct Knowledge Transfer for Offline Q-Learning

link.title: Direct Knowledge Transfer for Offline Q-Learning

entry.content:
Data-driven sequential decision making in marketing and healthcare can benefit from observations collected in related environments, particularly when data in the environment of interest are limited. Transferring such information requires accounting for differences in rewards and transition dynamics across environments. We study knowledge transfer for offline reinforcement learning through a joint estimation framework that directly integrates source information into target value-function learning. We propose Direct Transfer Fitted Q-Iteration (DFQI), which updates the target Q-function while simultaneously borrowing the source information through an L1 penalty that links the target coefficients to a weighted aggregate of source coefficients, with both determined jointly within each Bellman update. Using sieve approximation, we establish statistical guarantees for target estimation and policy learning in stationary discounted environments with common or heterogeneous transition kernels. Empirical studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DFQI framework in transferring source information to improve policy learning with limited target data.

Read more

entry.title: Directional Nonlinear Principal Components: a measure transportation approach

link.title: Directional Nonlinear Principal Components: a measure transportation approach

entry.content:
One of the earliest techniques in multivariate analysis, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) remains among the most popular ones in the area. PCA, however, is a linear and bidirectional technique (principal directions $\pm\mathbf{u}$ are defined up to a sign), which is fine under Gaussian or elliptical assumptions but constitutes a major limitation outside that restrictive context. This has prompted the development of numerous nonlinear approaches. We show here how recent results in measure transportation allow for a nonlinear and strictly directional (disentangling $\mathbf{u}$ and $-\mathbf{u}$) concept preserving the intuitive interpretation of the classical linear concept by maximizing expected squared arc lengths along data-driven principal curves rather than principal directions.

Read more

entry.title: Discretization approximation: An alternative to Monte Carlo in Bayesian computation

link.title: Discretization approximation: An alternative to Monte Carlo in Bayesian computation

entry.content:
In this paper we propose a new deterministic approximation method, called discretization approximation, for Bayesian computation. Discretization approximation is very simple to understand and to implement, It only requires calculating posterior density values as probability masses at pre-specified support points. The resulting discrete distribution can be a good approximation to the target posterior distribution. All posterior quantities, including means, standard deviations, and quantiles, can be approximated by those of this completely known discrete distribution. We establish the convergence rate of discretization approximation as the number of support points goes to infinity. If the support points are generated from quasi-Monte Carlo sequences, then the rate is actually the same as that in integration approximation, generally faster than the optimal statistical rate. In this sense, discretization approximation is superior to the popular Markov chain Monte Carlo method. We also provide random sampling and representation point construction methods from discretization approximation. Numerical examples including some benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method performs quite well for both low-dimensional and high-dimensional cases.

Read more

entry.title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk

link.title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk

entry.content:
Quantitative macroeconomics typically disciplines models by matching selected moments. We show how finite-state hidden Markov approximations make likelihood estimation and model selection feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes on short panels, without simulation. We illustrate the method with PSID earnings data. The calibrations that best match moments of earnings dynamics fit complete histories worse than a likelihood-estimated process with a Gaussian persistent component. In a standard saving model, calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of three. Close agreement with selected moments can leave economic predictions largely undetermined.

Read more

entry.title: Dynamic Multi-Pair Trading Strategy in Cryptocurrency Markets with Deep Reinforcement Learning

link.title: Dynamic Multi-Pair Trading Strategy in Cryptocurrency Markets with Deep Reinforcement Learning

entry.content:
This study aims to determine whether the application of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) as a specialized execution overlay can enhance pair trading in highly volatile cryptocurrency markets. Although classical implementations of the strategy have proven successful in traditional equities, they frequently exhibit rigidity and suffer from severe divergence risks when applied to high-variance environments. To construct a robust system, we developed a hierarchical “Filter-then-Rank” pair selection methodology and a custom “Fixed Risk, Adaptive Mean” execution model. The system employs a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layer to govern execution decisions within strict deterministic risk management boundaries. Evaluated on 1-hour interval data from the Binance USD-M Futures market, the selected RL policy achieved an Out-Of-Sample performance that substantially outperformed the heuristic baseline, although the results varied considerably across five random seeds, with four of the five seeds exceeding the baseline in both CAGR and Sortino Ratio. A stationary circular block bootstrap test of the Agent’s risk-adjusted outperformance yields p-values of approximately 0.06, which fall just short of the conventional 5% significance threshold. Ultimately, this study contributes to the quantitative finance literature by introducing a hybrid architecture that combines statistical arbitrage with DRL execution policies. Furthermore, it applies safe reinforcement learning via deterministic shielding, with results indicating that anchoring a neural policy to statistically robust boundaries mitigates severe divergence risks.

entry.title: Efficient Causal Survival Inference under Limited Surrogate Monitoring

link.title: Efficient Causal Survival Inference under Limited Surrogate Monitoring

entry.content:
Post-treatment surrogate endpoints can improve the efficiency of causal survival effect estimation, but their monitoring may end before follow-up for the primary outcome. We investigate the impact of limited recurrence monitoring on semiparametric efficiency when mortality follow-up continues. We derive the efficient influence function under limited monitoring and establish an exact expression for the efficiency gain from extending monitoring between any two durations. Our framework encompasses the absence of surrogate information and the usual shared-censoring scheme as boundary cases, and allows comparison with fully observed surrogates. We develop a doubly robust estimator under limited surrogate monitoring and establish asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency for its cross-fitted version under suitable conditions. Simulations and an application to breast cancer data illustrate the proposed method.

Read more

entry.title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches

link.title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches

entry.content:
Increased computing power has transformed computational science and improved predictive capabilities for complex systems, but many phenomena still exceed current simulation capabilities or require rapid evaluations for fast design iterations. Closure models address this challenge by approximating unresolved effects in reduced or incomplete dynamical systems. Data-driven closures offer a flexible mechanism for improving model accuracy and applicability, but approaches that embed the closure within a computational model for construction and training phases can be computationally expensive and cause numerical instabilities in the computational model during training. To avoid the challenges posed by embedded approaches, staged approaches to closure-model learning have been developed. The first stage uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations. The second stage trains a machine learning closure model offline using the assimilated data, thereby avoiding repeated simulator calls during training. In this work, we investigate the cost and accuracy tradeoffs between embedded and staged data-driven closure modeling approaches for a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure. The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.

Read more

entry.title: Efficient Proper Agnostic Learning of Halfspaces

link.title: Efficient Proper Agnostic Learning of Halfspaces

entry.content:
We give a proper membership-query algorithm for agnostically learning halfspaces under the uniform distribution on ${\pm1}^n$. Given query access to an arbitrary function $f:{\pm1}^n \to {\pm1}$, our algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)+2^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$ and outputs a halfspace with error at most $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the error of the best-fitting halfspace for $f$. Previously, even with membership queries, the best known running time was $n^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$, achieved by the sample-based algorithm of Kalai, Klivans, Mansour, and Servedio (FOCS 2005). Our algorithm is the first agnostic halfspace learner under the uniform distribution on ${\pm1}^n$ whose running time is polynomial in $n$ with an exponent independent of $\varepsilon$. Combining our algorithm with a boosting argument yields a proper agnostic learner using only random examples. It achieves the same $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$ guarantee, with running time matching that of Kalai et al.\ up to an additive term depending only on $\varepsilon$. To our knowledge, this is the first sample-based proper agnostic learner in the Boolean setting with running time $2^{o(n)}$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.

entry.title: Empirical rather than simulated spectral band adjustment of MODIS to Sentinel-3 OLCI for European vegetation monitoring

link.title: Empirical rather than simulated spectral band adjustment of MODIS to Sentinel-3 OLCI for European vegetation monitoring

entry.content:
Spectral band adjustment derived from convolved spectra describes sensor differences under controlled conditions, but its applicability to operational products requires assessment. We compare this approach with adjustment estimated directly from MODIS and Sentinel-3 OLCI observations for European vegetation monitoring. Both streams undergo atmospheric correction and Ross-Thick/Li-Sparse Reciprocal BRDF normalization to nadir viewing and local solar noon. Using observations from 2019-2024, we derive annual OLCI/MODIS reflectance-ratio relationships with unadjusted MODIS NDVI. The operational correction uses quadratic red and linear near-infrared (NIR) functions. We compare these relationships with irradiance-weighted canopy simulations and assess the empirical correction at 460 locations. Simulated and empirical relationships differ, particularly for red reflectance at high NDVI. Background-dependent simulated ratios also demonstrate the limitations of a single NDVI-based function. The empirical correction reduces red and NIR root-mean-square error (RMSE) at 66.3% and 71.1% of locations, with median paired reductions of 5.98% and 13.67%. Median paired RMSE decreases by 0.86% for NDVI but increases by 0.95% for EVI2, 0.74% for NIRv and 7.07% for the Plant Phenology Index (PPI), calculated with stream-specific historical references. This study establishes an operational empirical adjustment and shows that the specified spectral simulation does not reproduce the relationship between the normalized products. It provides evidence for improved reflectance consistency while demonstrating that vegetation-index benefits require separate assessment.

entry.title: Error Accumulation in Second-Order Sequential Machine Unlearning

link.title: Error Accumulation in Second-Order Sequential Machine Unlearning

entry.content:
Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of deleted training data without full retraining. In the sequential setting, deletion requests arrive over time, and repeated updates can accumulate approximation errors. In this paper, we study error accumulation in high dimensions, where parameter count $p$ is proportional to sample size $n$, for second-order unlearning methods under two privacy settings: (i) \emph{partial unlearning}, which allows unpublished internal states to be retained while certified versions of the model are released; and (ii) \emph{perfect unlearning}, which retains only published models and no hidden states. We also distinguish pointwise and pathwise certification, depending on whether the certification guarantee applies to each released model or the whole released sequence. We analyze conjugate gradient (CG) as an efficient solver for the inverse Hessian-vector product (IHVP) in Newton iterations. Our theory shows that a maximum of 1/2/2/3 Newton–CG updates suffice for successful certification and vanishing population-risk degradation of the published model, for pointwise partial, pathwise partial, pointwise perfect and pathwise perfect certification, respectively. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate sequential tracking and substantial computational gains of Newton-based methods combined with conjugate gradient, over gradient-based updates, especially for ill-conditioned problems.

Read more

entry.title: Estimating Average Treatment Effects with Projected Instrumental Variables

link.title: Estimating Average Treatment Effects with Projected Instrumental Variables

entry.content:
In this paper, we develop a projected instrumental variable framework that relaxes conventional assumptions for causal identification with instrumental variables. Building on the interpretation of conditional expectation as an orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space, the framework replaces the conditional expectation operator with a general projection operator. We provide an alternative inverse problem formulation based on the Riesz representation. Drawing on semiparametric efficiency theory, we further develop debiased and adaptive machine learning methods for estimation and inference. The proposed framework connects invalid instrumental variables to instrumented difference-in-differences. We also examine invalid projected instrumental variables and discuss their relationship to existing methods. Simulation studies and real data analysis demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably compared with existing approaches.

Read more

entry.title: Eunoia: Area-Proportional Euler and Venn Diagrams in Rust, Julia, Python, R, and JavaScript

link.title: Eunoia: Area-Proportional Euler and Venn Diagrams in Rust, Julia, Python, R, and JavaScript

entry.content:
Area-proportional Euler diagrams visualize sets and their intersections through regions whose areas represent their sizes. Because many set specifications have no exact geometric representation, constructing these diagrams requires numerical optimization and diagnostics that quantify the remaining discrepancies. Eunoia is a Rust library for fitting area-proportional Euler diagrams and constructing canonical Venn diagrams. It supports circles, ellipses, squares, and rectangles, computes region areas analytically, and provides exact analytical gradients for several shape families. Its fitting pipeline combines multidimensional scaling initialization with local refinement, global optimization when needed, and seeded restarts. Fitted layouts include residuals and goodness-of-fit statistics that help users assess how faithfully a diagram represents the data. Shared plotting routines extract region polygons, place labels, and pack unit glyphs and member names within regions. The same core implementation powers packages for R, Python, Julia, and JavaScript, a C interface, and a web application that fits diagrams entirely in the browser through WebAssembly. By centralizing fitting, geometry, diagnostics, and annotation in an independent library, Eunoia provides consistent set visualization across programming languages and interactive applications.

Read more

entry.title: Evaluation of clinical prediction models: Decomposing performance uncertainty into model development and validation components

link.title: Evaluation of clinical prediction models: Decomposing performance uncertainty into model development and validation components

entry.content:
There has been growing emphasis on acknowledging, quantifying, and communicating the uncertainty inherent in the output of clinical prediction models. However, allowing for model uncertainty when assessing the performance of an existing model in a new sample (i.e., external validation) has not been sufficiently explored. When validating a model that generates uncertain predictions, the uncertainty of a given performance metric is affected by both model uncertainty and the finiteness of the validation sample (validation uncertainty). For a given performance metric, we show that the total uncertainty of the performance estimate can be decomposed into the uncertainty due to the model and the uncertainty due to the validation. Also, we propose $M^2$, the fraction of the total variance due to model uncertainty, and $V^2$, the fraction of the total variance due to validation uncertainty. These measures serve as complementary scalar indices that can be implemented for common performance metrics and visualizations such as calibration plots using simple Monte Carlo algorithms. Critically, our case study shows that with the same model and the same validation sample, the contribution of uncertainty sources is highly variable across performance metrics ($M^2$ varying from 12% for the Brier score to 78% for the calibration slope). This indicates that stakeholders who prioritize different aspects of performance (e.g., calibration versus clinical utility) might arrive at different decisions on whether future efforts should be directed towards creating a more reliable model or procuring a larger validation sample. In conclusion, external validation studies can readily be amended to incorporate model uncertainty, and we recommend that such studies report total variance as well as the relative share of variance components for all performance metrics.

Read more

entry.title: EventGPT: Next-Event Pretraining on Banking Customer Histories

link.title: EventGPT: Next-Event Pretraining on Banking Customer Histories

entry.content:
A model pretrained to predict a customer’s next event can estimate the probability of future events without training on their labels and provide a reusable representation for supervised downstream banking tasks. We pretrain EventGPT, a hierarchical causal transformer, by next-token maximum likelihood estimation on the public Multimodal Banking Dataset (MBD-mini: 100,224 clients, 38.8 million transactions and 66.3 million geolocation pings). Keeping one state per event, EventGPT trains in about two hours on one L4 GPU at windows up to 8,192 tokens. From its next-event distribution, with no labels, EventGPT scores five targets of the form “the client makes a transaction of a given kind for the first time next month” at ROC-AUC 0.79 to 0.92. Gradient boosting on 114 engineered features needs 10,000 to 300,000 labeled client-months to match it on four targets and stays below it on the fifth. For product prediction, frozen EventGPT embeddings score below the engineered features (mean ROC-AUC 0.787 against 0.808 over five test folds), and a rank-averaged ensemble of EventGPT, profile fields and token counts with the engineered features adds 0.014 to 0.017, of which 0.007 to 0.016 is EventGPT’s own. The code and pretrained weights are released.

Read more

entry.title: Exact Fusion of Softmax Attention Heads Can Require Exponentially Many Atoms

link.title: Exact Fusion of Softmax Attention Heads Can Require Exponentially Many Atoms

entry.content:
Fusing independently normalized attention heads can increase the number of explicit key-value entries, or atoms, needed to preserve their output. We prove a sharp separation for $W_d(q)=\sum_{j=1}^d\sigma(q_j)$: its $d$ two-atom heads use $2d$ head-atom terms, whereas its minimum single-head representation has exactly $2^d$ atoms, even with arbitrary fixed replacement keys, scalar values, and positive masses. The same lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below $1/2$ on $\mathbb R^d$, and the threshold is sharp. The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; exact equality on any nonempty open query domain inherits the bound. The resulting atom bound for a fixed head count is tight when that count divides $d$. A normalized family retains its exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls. For pretrained-model caches, a classical affine-rank bound and a certified instance exclude exact vector preservation at a specified atom count. Learned-cache comparisons on two disjoint banks of 64 contexts show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects.

Read more

entry.title: Exact, Nonparametric Sensitivity Analysis for Observational Studies of Contingency Tables

link.title: Exact, Nonparametric Sensitivity Analysis for Observational Studies of Contingency Tables

entry.content:
In observational studies, contingency tables are commonly used to examine associations between categorical variables. However, any test of association in contingency tables may be biased by unmeasured confounding, and existing sensitivity analyses typically assume a binary treatment or impose strong parametric assumptions on non-binary treatments. We develop an exact (non-asymptotic) and nonparametric sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding in $I \times J$ and $I\times J\times K$ contingency tables, accommodating both non-binary treatments and outcomes. Extending Rosenbaum’s generic bias sensitivity model, we derive a general method to compute the exact worst-case null distribution for any count-based test, including chi-squared and likelihood-based tests of association. We further provide specialized results for subfamilies of count-based tests that enable more efficient computation of the worst-case null distribution. Finally, we investigate test power in sensitivity analyses and show that tests exploiting all treatment and outcome levels achieve higher power than tests that dichotomize the categorical variables. We illustrate the proposed methods with a re-analysis of the effect of pre-kindergarten care on math achievement using data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study. The R package sensitivityIxJ that implements the method is on CRAN.

Read more

entry.title: Exact Simes inequalities for two-sided Gaussian tests

link.title: Exact Simes inequalities for two-sided Gaussian tests

entry.content:
The Simes test combines marginal p-values to test a global null hypothesis. Whether it controls the type I error for two-sided Gaussian tests with arbitrary covariance remains open. We prove that, for every fixed number $m$ of tests, the rejection probability does not exceed the nominal level when that level is sufficiently small. The same range of levels works for every covariance matrix. Equality holds if and only if the p-values form independent groups with identical values within each group. For $m=3$, a computer-assisted proof establishes validity at $0.05$, and an analytic argument extends it to an explicit interval around $0.05$. As the number $m$ of tests increases, we prove validity in two settings: each test statistic is correlated with at most a fixed number of others; or the statistics form independent blocks whose sizes grow sufficiently slowly, at a specified rate of order $\log\log m$. Both settings allow arbitrary correlations within these restrictions. For any fixed $0<1$, validity holds for every $m$ above a threshold $M$ and every level $0<\alpha\le a$; the same $M$ works for all allowed covariances. Further results quantify the difference between the nominal level and the rejection probability, and permit more correlated neighbors when their correlations are bounded away from $\pm1$. We do not obtain numerical values for the general small-level cutoffs or the required number of tests.

Read more

entry.title: Exploiting Locally Exogeneous Variation in Spatial Data: Linear Regression with Many Small Units

link.title: Exploiting Locally Exogeneous Variation in Spatial Data: Linear Regression with Many Small Units

entry.content:
This article shows how researchers can exploit \textit{locally exogeneous variation} even in the presence of endogeneity, autocorrelation, or spurious correlation. It describes the infill asymptotic properties of generalized least squares estimation with county-level data, Census tract-level data, and similar regional averages, including sufficient conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality, and valid inference.

entry.title: Fast nonparametric estimation of sparse precision matrices with a priori sparsity structure

link.title: Fast nonparametric estimation of sparse precision matrices with a priori sparsity structure

entry.content:
This work describes a computational approach for rapidly estimating and characterizing the covariance structure of a Gaussian random field from a modest number of i.i.d. replicates by formulating the problem in terms of a sparse inverse Cholesky factor of the data’s covariance matrix. Borrowing from the extensive literature of using directed acyclic graphs to impose sparsity on inverse Cholesky factors (for example, Vecchia’s approximation or nearest-neighbor Gaussian process models), a probabilistically parsimonious a priori sparsity pattern is imposed, and with careful formulation the estimation problem is given as an extremely well-structured convex problem that can be solved for millions of unknowns in seconds on a single processor core. After describing the problem and specific formulation of the optimization, we demonstrate the estimator’s speed and effectiveness at capturing a variety of nonstationary structures in spatial or spatio-temporal data, and in ensemble data assimilation.

Read more

entry.title: Features Extraction Across Multi-Source Heterogeneous Data

link.title: Features Extraction Across Multi-Source Heterogeneous Data

entry.content:
High-dimensional data from multiple sources often combine shared structure with source-specific variation. We study heterogeneous principal component analysis, which seeks to recover common and private principal subspaces when their dimensions are unknown. {We propose \emph{Feature Extraction (FE)}, a novel data-driven framework with two steps. First, the Eigenvector-based Spike-Count (ESC) estimator determines the number of principal components (PC) in each source using only sample eigenvector information, rather than eigenvalue-based criteria. Second, FE identifies the locations of common features by comparing bias-corrected inner products between sample eigenvectors across sources. These matches yield estimates of the common and source-specific subspaces without iterative optimization. We establish the consistency of our estimators under a spiked covariance model in a high-dimensional regime where the dimension and sample size grow proportionally. Simulations and applications to federated image data and U.S. housing prices demonstrate the performance of FE in rank recovery, subspace estimation, and data reconstruction.} Code is available at https://github.com/liwenbo-research/HeterogeneousPCA

Read more

entry.title: Federated Estimation of Loading Spaces in Tensor Factor Models under Differential Privacy

link.title: Federated Estimation of Loading Spaces in Tensor Factor Models under Differential Privacy

entry.content:
Tensor factor models provide low-dimensional representations of tensor-valued observations while preserving their multiway structure. When these observations are held by different clients, privacy constraints may prevent them from being pooled for centralized analysis. We study estimation of common loading spaces in Tucker tensor factor models under federated differential privacy, allowing heterogeneous sample sizes, privacy budgets, and factor strengths. The proposed method combines private stability testing, Huber aggregation, and Gaussian perturbation at each client with weighted aggregation at the server. We establish non-asymptotic upper bounds governed by a scaled harmonic mean of the squared local error rates, and prove minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors under strong factors, fixed factor ranks, and fixed noise variance. We further develop a private calibration procedure that selects the local tuning parameters and aggregation weights without knowledge of the noise level or client-specific factor strengths. The resulting adaptive estimator preserves the privacy guarantee and attains the error rate obtained with oracle tuning. We illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators through simulation experiments and an application to a Meditation Traits EEG dataset.

Read more

entry.title: Finite-Sample Calibration and Power Benchmarks in Two-Sample Random-Integration Tests

link.title: Finite-Sample Calibration and Power Benchmarks in Two-Sample Random-Integration Tests

entry.content:
In high-dimensional two-group studies, a supplied variable set can be used directly or to learn a projection. We study how much attainable power these choices retain at fixed observation and calibration budgets. For complete unbiased random-integration statistics under Gaussian common shape, a fixed-spectrum comparison orders direction-wise power and gives an explicit criterion balancing an oracle advantage against learning loss. Joint regeneration controls level for a specified learner with unknown diagonal shape. A paired construction permits observation reuse and finite-reference calibration of fitted scores and menus. In the paired diagonal experiment, an invariant sparse likelihood-ratio benchmark provides an attainable efficiency target. Finite-amplitude bounds connect a classical bounded quadratic to this target; conditioning on the coordinate maximum yields informative complementary bounds at moderate and strong signals. Both comparisons include finite reference budgets, and null-only simulations certify local comparisons with specified fitted rules. Equal-budget experiments and a leukemia application compare aggregation, projection and fitted quadratic scores. For correlated paired data, classical sign randomization supplies a separate calibration under central symmetry. The efficiency guarantees apply to the stated experiments and signal classes; general small-budget shape efficiency and adaptation to unknown signal allocation remain open.

Read more

entry.title: Finite-sample Valid Permutation Inference under Multi-way Clustering

link.title: Finite-sample Valid Permutation Inference under Multi-way Clustering

entry.content:
Econometric applications with multi-way clustering often feature a small number of effective clusters or heavy-tailed data, making standard cluster-robust and bootstrap inference unreliable in finite samples. In this paper, we develop a framework for finite-sample valid permutation inference in linear regression with multi-way clustering under an assumption of conditional exchangeability of the errors. Our assumption is closely related to the notion of separate exchangeability studied in earlier work, but can be more realistic in many economic settings as it imposes minimal restrictions on the covariate distribution. We construct permutation tests of significance that are valid in finite samples and establish theoretical power guarantees, in contrast to existing methods that are justified only asymptotically. While our main presentation is under exchangeable errors, our framework encompasses invariance-based tests that remain valid under general forms of heteroskedastic errors. We also extend our methodology to settings with missing data and derive power results that reveal phase transitions in detectability. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate that the proposed tests maintain correct size and competitive power, while standard cluster-robust and bootstrap procedures can exhibit substantial size distortions.

Read more

entry.title: Fixed-smoothing Uniform Inference for Quantile Regression

link.title: Fixed-smoothing Uniform Inference for Quantile Regression

entry.content:
This paper develops fixed-smoothing inference methods for time-series quantile regression that are robust to heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation. Our approach is uniformly valid over quantile levels and accounts for dependence over time and across quantiles. It enables uniform confidence bands, Wald and Sup-t tests for joint hypotheses, and tests of shape restrictions, providing a unified framework for assessing heterogeneity in quantile effects. Under weak dependence, uniform inference for quantile regression processes is non-pivotal because the limiting distributions depend on the long-run covariance structure across quantiles. To address this issue, we develop two complementary approaches. The uniform-in-$\tau$ method estimates this structure and simulates the non-pivotal limiting distribution. For certain tests involving finitely many quantiles, the stack-Wald method delivers pivotal fixed-smoothing inference. We establish the asymptotic validity of both approaches. Simulations show improved size control over existing HAC-based procedures while maintaining good power. An application to stock-return prediction reveals substantial heterogeneity in predictive effects.

Read more

entry.title: Flow Matching for Count Data

link.title: Flow Matching for Count Data

entry.content:
High-dimensional count data arise in applications such as single-cell RNA sequencing and neural spike trains, where mappings between distributions across successive batches or time points form critical components of data analysis. The recent success of diffusion- and flow-based deep generative models for images, video, and text motivates extending these ideas to count-valued settings, but many existing methods either treat each count as a categorical state or transform counts into a continuous space, neither of which is natural or efficient when the count range is large. We propose count-FM, a flow-matching framework for count data based on a continuous-time birth-death process with local unit jumps. Count-FM learns marginal transitions efficiently in count space through simulation-free training of conditional transition rates, allowing transport between arbitrary count-distributed source and target populations. In simulation, count-FM variants achieve strong sample quality while using substantially fewer parameters. We further apply count-FM to scRNA-seq and neural spike-train data for unconditional generation, transport, and conditional generation. Across these tasks, count-FM yields improved sample quality, greater modeling efficiency, and interpretable transport paths.

Read more

entry.title: Functional Principal Component Analysis for Manifold-Indexed Data

link.title: Functional Principal Component Analysis for Manifold-Indexed Data

entry.content:
Functional principal component analysis has traditionally focused on processes indexed by Euclidean domains, although functional observations increasingly arise on curved domains. We develop functional principal component analysis for real-valued processes observed at discrete locations on a general Riemannian manifold. We estimate the mean and covariance functions using intrinsic kernel smoothing based on geodesic distance and a normal-coordinate volume correction, with a general weighting scheme accommodating unequal numbers of observations across subjects. We establish $L^2$ and uniform convergence rates for these estimators and derive corresponding error bounds for the estimated eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. These results quantify how manifold dimension, sampling frequency and the weighting scheme affect estimation accuracy and characterize the phase transition between sparse and dense sampling regimes. Simulation studies on the circle and sphere, together with real-data applications, illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology.

Read more

entry.title: Generalization Error Bounds for Picard-Type Operator Learning in Nonlinear Parabolic PDEs

link.title: Generalization Error Bounds for Picard-Type Operator Learning in Nonlinear Parabolic PDEs

entry.content:
Operator learning for partial differential equations (PDEs) aims to learn solution operators on infinite-dimensional function spaces from finite-resolution data. In this setting, it is important for the learned model to be discretization-invariant, or resolution-robust, and to reflect PDE-specific structure. It is therefore natural to ask how such structure should be encoded in the model architecture, hypothesis class, or learning procedure. In this paper, we study operator learning for solution operators of nonlinear parabolic PDEs based on Duhamel–Picard iteration. We formulate Picard iteration as an abstract state-transition model and present a theoretical framework for Picard-type operator learning. We derive implementation-agnostic generalization error bounds that separate the implementation error from the estimation error associated with the abstract state-transition model induced by Picard iteration. A key consequence is that increasing the Picard depth reduces the Picard truncation error without causing an unbounded growth of the entropy-based estimation error. We also extend the analysis to long-time prediction by rolling out the same learned local model over successive time blocks. Finally, we illustrate the theory for nonlinear heat equations on the torus using a Picard-type Fourier neural operator as a concrete implementation.

Read more

entry.title: Geodesics and intrinsic statistics of isolated connections in Hermitian positive-definite matrices

link.title: Geodesics and intrinsic statistics of isolated connections in Hermitian positive-definite matrices

entry.content:
Quantifying change in a single covariance, coherence or spectral connection requires a distance that respects the positive-definiteness constraint and holds the surrounding entries fixed. We characterize the Riemannian geometry induced by the affine-invariant metric when one conjugate off-diagonal pair of a Hermitian positive-definite matrix varies under this constraint. A fixed Schur congruence maps the admissible set to an open complex disk and reduces its metric to a two-dimensional form independent of the ambient matrix dimension. The disk is complete, with Gaussian curvature in $(-1/4,0]$, and has unique minimizing geodesics and globally defined logarithms. Its intrinsic distance strictly exceeds the ambient affine-invariant distance between distinct points. Conservation of angular momentum reduces the geodesic boundary-value problem to a single scalar equation with elementary angular and length integrals, enabling distance and logarithm evaluation without shooting. For a declared reference distribution with a finite second intrinsic moment, we establish a unique Fr'echet centre and consistency of its empirical estimate, together with a sandwich central limit theorem under the stated regularity conditions. Tangent covariance standardization yields moment identities, and exchangeable rank calibration supplies finite-sample score guarantees. These results provide a geometric and statistical framework for isolated connections on a fixed complement, with explicit limits on extension to varying complements.

Read more

entry.title: Global Convergence of Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares for Robust Subspace Recovery

link.title: Global Convergence of Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares for Robust Subspace Recovery

entry.content:
Robust subspace estimation is fundamental to many machine learning and data analysis tasks. Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) is an elegant and empirically effective approach to this problem, yet its theoretical properties remain poorly understood. This paper establishes that, under deterministic conditions, a variant of IRLS with dynamic smoothing regularization converges linearly to the underlying subspace from any initialization. We extend these guarantees to affine subspace estimation, a setting that lacks prior recovery theory. Additionally, we illustrate the practical benefits of IRLS through an application to low-dimensional neural network training. Our results provide the first global convergence guarantees for IRLS in robust subspace recovery and, more broadly, for nonconvex IRLS on a Riemannian manifold.

Read more

entry.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference

link.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference

entry.content:
Anaerobic digestion (AD) models can be challenging to calibrate against real data due to limited practical identifiability, data scarcity, and model complexity. Weighted least squares objective functions and gradient-based solvers using finite differences are often used in literature, but result in suboptimal parameter estimates and large uncertainty bands. This paper identifies the parameters of a reduced-order ADM1 by comparing the frameworks of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and Bayesian inference (BI), and quantifies uncertainties of parameters and outputs. Multirate experimental data are taken from a lab-scale AD reactor fed with agricultural substrates and operated at organic loading rates of 3$\,$g VS $\mathrm{m^{-3}d^{-1}}$. Global optima are found via global and gradient-based local search algorithms using forward sensitivities. Enhanced scatter search provides the best global search results. These are refined by the Gauss-Newton algorithm as the best local search, which delivers $R^2$ values of 0.95 for acetic acid and 0.77 for biogas production. BI yields substantially narrower uncertainty bands than MLE and avoids the need for a global search by incorporating prior knowledge about parameter distributions. The search space is captured efficiently by log10 scaling of parameters. Algorithmic details on its implications are provided. Despite a high-resolution lab-scale dataset, the ADM1-specific inhibition parameter $K_\mathrm{I,nh3}$ is practically not identifiable with MLE, and shows a low output sensitivity, whereas a parameter for the effective ion concentration shows superb practical identifiabilty at high confidence with both MLE and BI. The present work lays a scalable base for calibration of nonlinear AD models by providing reliable simulations. It thus advances model-based monitoring and control applications of multirate processes such as agricultural AD plants.

Read more

entry.title: Graph-Based Testing of Conditional Mean Independence with Applications to Large Language Model Evaluation

link.title: Graph-Based Testing of Conditional Mean Independence with Applications to Large Language Model Evaluation

entry.content:
We study whether a predictor $X$ provides additional information for predicting a scalar response $Y$ after adjustment for other variables $Z$, formalized by testing $\mathsf{H}_0:\E(Y\mid X,Z)=\E(Y\mid Z)$. Existing methods often require estimating nuisance functions involving $X$, which can be difficult for high-dimensional or structured predictors. We propose a graph-based test that extends the edge count principle to covariate adjustment. It represents $X$ through pairwise dissimilarities, estimates only the baseline regression $\E(Y\mid Z)$, and aggregates products of held-out residuals across graph edges. We develop sample-splitting and two-fold cross-fitting versions. Under regularity conditions, both have standard normal null limits, yielding analytic $p$-values, and are consistent under graph-smooth and graph-rough alternatives. Simulations with vector, image, and network predictors show good size control and power advantages over competing procedures, with cross-fitting improving power across the main alternatives. Applications examine human quality ratings, mathematical error labels, and LLM response preferences. Our method detects associations with quality ratings and an LLM judge’s preferences after adjustment for text length and other recorded characteristics.

Read more

entry.title: HALO: Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records

link.title: HALO: Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records

entry.content:
Learning from extensive longitudinal clinical records–spanning repeated encounters, evolving conditions, and heterogeneous documentation–under a finite labeling budget requires solving two coupled problems: deciding what evidence to keep and deciding which patients deserve higher-fidelity labels. Prior work on active learning and multi-fidelity label acquisition mainly addresses the second problem, while treating the evidence presented to the acquisition policy as fixed. We present HALO, a Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning pipeline for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records. This framework jointly learns what to read and what label source to acquire under budget. HALO first selects informative evidence from longitudinal records and then uses a budget-aware policy to allocate free-, silver-, and gold-fidelity label sources. For frozen policies, our theory characterizes asymmetric acquired-label channels and gives a budget-constrained finite-sample gold-risk bound for a common downstream logistic model. In a heart-failure case study, HALO attained the highest MedAlign acquired-label F1 at six of eight target budgets. A downstream classifier trained on HALO-acquired labels attained the highest external MGB F1 at budgets 15-60 and remained within 0.01 of the best comparator at budgets 75-120.

Read more

A downstream classifier trained on HALO-acquired labels attained the highest external MGB F1 at budgets 15-60 and remained within 0.01 of the best comparator at budgets 75-120.

entry.title: High-Frequency Estimation of the Leverage Effect under Rough Volatility with Microstructure Noise

link.title: High-Frequency Estimation of the Leverage Effect under Rough Volatility with Microstructure Noise

entry.content:
This paper develops feasible high-frequency inference for the leverage effect when the spot variance follows rough Volterra dynamics, leverage loadings depend on endogenous rough states, and observed prices may be contaminated by microstructure noise. We define an integrated leverage parameter through a scaled covariation between log prices and spot variance that accounts for their different local fluctuation scales. The scaled realized covariation admits a stable functional central limit theorem with an explicit pathwise centering correction arising from within-interval variation in the leverage loading. A loading regularity condition renders this correction asymptotically negligible, and we verify the condition for direct Volterra loadings and for smooth functions of closed rough states for every Hurst index below one half. We construct a block-based estimator with an exact finite-window correction for the leading proportional bias, together with a nonnegative single-scale estimator of its asymptotic variance. Pre-averaging extends feasible inference to observations with independent and identically distributed microstructure noise. Simulations under the rough Heston model demonstrate accurate finite-sample calibration with and without noise. An empirical application to fifteen years of one-second data on nine U.S. equities and ETFs finds negative median leverage estimates for every asset at weekly and monthly horizons.

Read more

entry.title: High-dimensional Autoregressive Modeling for Time Series with Hierarchical Structures

link.title: High-dimensional Autoregressive Modeling for Time Series with Hierarchical Structures

entry.content:
High-dimensional data, especially time-dependent data with increasingly complex structures, have become ubiquitous in modern applications, and hierarchical relationships among variables are increasingly common. However, there is still a lack of supervised learning tools in the literature for them. To fill this gap, we introduce a new model-designing framework, and it then combines with unsupervised factor modeling tools to form an efficient and interpretable autoregressive model for high-dimensional time series with hierarchical structures. An ordinary least squares estimation is considered, and its non-asymptotic properties are established. Moreover, we propose an algorithm to search for estimates, and a boosting method is also suggested for hyperparameter selection. Simulation experiments are conducted to evaluate finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology, and its usefulness is demonstrated by an application to the Personality-120 dataset.

Read more

entry.title: How Does Chain-of-Thought Supervision Teach Models to Reason? A Theoretical Analysis

link.title: How Does Chain-of-Thought Supervision Teach Models to Reason? A Theoretical Analysis

entry.content:
Training with chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision is an effective approach for teaching models multi-step reasoning procedures. At inference time, however, models may need to continue reasoning beyond the finite teacher CoT sequences observed during training, and longer reasoning can instead degrade performance, a phenomenon known as overthinking. How the amount and structure of training-time CoT give rise to such failures remains theoretically poorly understood. To study this problem, we introduce an in-context weight prediction model trained on finite gradient descent trajectories for linear regression. Using high-dimensional asymptotic analysis, we show that the success and failure modes of long-horizon reasoning undergo phase transitions depending on the context length and the total amount of training CoT. We further distinguish two mechanisms of overthinking, error accumulation and error amplification, and show that with short training contexts, increasing the training CoT budget can worsen long-horizon error before eventually stabilizing reasoning. Experiments with fully trained linear and multi-head softmax attention further show that these qualitative behaviors persist. Our results provide a theoretical account linking properties of training-time CoT to inference-time failures and offer guidance for designing teacher CoT that supports stable reasoning.

entry.title: Hybrid Federated Learning for Multimodal Fusion under Missing Modalities and Site Heterogeneity

link.title: Hybrid Federated Learning for Multimodal Fusion under Missing Modalities and Site Heterogeneity

entry.content:
Multimodal fusion is studied under hybrid federation, where data are partitioned across samples and feature blocks. The proposed two-dimensional federated smooth multiple-kernel large-margin learning method (2D-FedSMKL) integrates availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation. For fixed maps and propensities, the objective is convex and smooth. Curvature bounds and exact synchronous block-gradient equivalence are established for binary and multiclass scores, giving a conditional accelerated rate. An oracle-propensity binary risk bound and a propensity-perturbation result are also derived. Simulations and two public activity-recognition benchmarks assess site heterogeneity and modality absence. Worst-site aggregation improves worst-site performance under heterogeneity, including reversed and size-balanced designs. On the benchmarks, validation selects the correction; the selected model is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site, and group-regularization benefits vary by dataset.

entry.title: Impact Range Assessment (IRA): An Interpretable Sensitivity Measure for Machine Learning Regression Modelling

link.title: Impact Range Assessment (IRA): An Interpretable Sensitivity Measure for Machine Learning Regression Modelling

entry.content:
While machine learning regression models capture the relationship between predictors and the response variable, they often lack intuitive methods to help modelers understand how sensitive model predictions are to changes in individual predictors. To address this limitation, we introduce a model-agnostic interpretability method called Impact Range Assessment (IRA), which quantifies the sensitivity of model predictions to changes in each predictor by measuring the range of predicted responses as the predictor varies across its observed range. Validation using synthetic linear and nonlinear datasets demonstrates that relevant predictors produced higher IRA values than irrelevant ones. Moreover, repeated evaluations produced results aligned with those from the single-execution analysis, confirming the method’s robustness. For demonstration, two benchmark datasets were used to evaluate IRA across five machine learning regression models, yielding model-specific sensitivity rankings and supporting IRA’s applicability as a complementary sensitivity analysis tool alongside feature importance methods such as permutation feature importance and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP).

Read more
