entry.title: Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis

link.title: Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis

entry.content:
Diffusion policies represent multimodal action distributions, but a $Q$-weighted update does not specify how to sample from the resulting target distribution. We propose Schr"odinger–F"ollmer Actor–Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) method for Kullback–Leibler (KL)-regularized policy improvement through conditional diffusion. A minimax Bellman critic estimates the action-value function, which defines an exponentially tilted target policy. A Doob $h$-transform expresses this update as a correction to the reference diffusion drift. The target drift is a weighted conditional mean of Brownian-bridge labels. We fit it by weighted regression using endpoints from the current policy and pointwise action-value evaluations. In the small-update regime, the KL-regularized update follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts. Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds that separate the errors from critic estimation, weighted neural drift regression, and diffusion discretization through a reverse-KL actor bound. The average-performance bound depends explicitly on the comparison coefficients over the policy iterations. Synthetic experiments assess approximation to prescribed advantage-tilted targets and sensitivity to the diffusion-step count. Across six offline-to-online continuous-control tasks, the $Q$-guided bridge-regression implementation achieves higher final-checkpoint returns than its BC initialization after $500K$ online interactions.

Read more

entry.title: Searching for related contributors to a DNA mixture using single cell analysis

link.title: Searching for related contributors to a DNA mixture using single cell analysis

entry.content:
We propose a staged process for assessing the presence of related individuals in an autosomal STR DNA mixture sample, when it is analysed using a single cell pipeline analysis (as opposed to a bulk mixture analysis). In the absence of a large dataset if single cells from real related people, artificial single cell data is generated by sampling individual locus data taken from single cell dataset of real unrelated people. It is applied to create random admixtures used in a relatedness search for pairs of individuals to illustrate the usefulness of the method.

Read more

author.name: Robert Cowell

entry.summary: We propose a staged process for assessing the presence of related individuals in an autosomal STR DNA mixture sample, when it is analysed using a single cell pipeline analysis (as opposed to a bulk mixture analysis). In the absence of a large dataset if single cells from real related people, artificial single cell data is generated by sampling individual locus data taken from single cell dataset of real unrelated people. It is applied to create random admixtures used in a relatedness search for pairs of individuals to illustrate the usefulness of the method.

entry.title: Second-Order Least Squares Method for Statistical Inference in Linear Models with Asymmetric Errors

link.title: Second-Order Least Squares Method for Statistical Inference in Linear Models with Asymmetric Errors

entry.content:
In a linear regression model with normal random errors, the ordinary least squares estimator is the most efficient estimator. However, when the random errors have an asymmetric distribution, a more efficient estimator can be constructed using the higher moments of the data. In this paper, we use the second-order least squares method to obtain more accurate asymptotic confidence intervals and more powerful hypothesis tests in linear models. We also develop an efficient and stable numerical algorithm to calculate the proposed estimator. Our extensive simulation studies demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method. Two real data examples are presented.

Read more

entry.title: Selecting Hyperparameters for Tree-Boosting

link.title: Selecting Hyperparameters for Tree-Boosting

entry.content:
Tree-boosting is a widely used machine learning technique for tabular data. However, its out-of-sample accuracy is critically dependent on multiple hyperparameters. In this article, we empirically compare several popular methods for hyperparameter optimization for tree-boosting including random grid search, the tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE), Gaussian-process-based Bayesian optimization (GP-BO), Hyperband, the sequential model-based algorithm configuration (SMAC) method, and deterministic full grid search using $59$ regression and binary classification data sets. We find that the SMAC method clearly outperforms all the other considered methods on average, and it gives stable performance across a diverse collection of tabular data sets under a fixed tuning budget, which is relevant for users who cannot afford extensive manual trial-and-error tuning. We further observe that (i) a relatively large number of trials larger than $100$ is typically required for accurate tuning, (ii) using default values for hyperparameters or a full search over a small grid often yields very inaccurate models, (iii) all considered hyperparameters can have a material effect on the accuracy of tree-boosting, i.e., there is no small set of hyperparameters that is more important than others, and (iv) choosing the number of boosting iterations using early stopping yields more accurate results compared to including it in the search space for regression tasks.

Read more

entry.title: Selective Randomization Inference for Interference

link.title: Selective Randomization Inference for Interference

entry.content:
Empirical researchers often use tests for interference as pretests or robustness checks. However, when the results guide the choice of models, parameters, or hypotheses, the resulting data-dependent selection can compromise the validity of subsequent inference. This paper develops a two-stage selective randomization inference framework for interference that explicitly conditions on the selection event to account for data-dependent selection. We first test the null hypothesis of no treatment spillover using a conditional randomization method. If this null is rejected, we test the null hypothesis of zero exposure contrast under a pre-specified exposure mapping that allows for spillover effects; otherwise, we test the null hypothesis of no direct effects under the assumption of no spillover. We prove that each second-stage test controls the selective Type I error rate in finite samples and evaluate the size and power of the proposed tests through Monte Carlo experiments.

Read more

entry.title: Selective inference for pruned interaction trees with known unequal variances in randomized trials

link.title: Selective inference for pruned interaction trees with known unequal variances in randomized trials

entry.content:
Interaction trees reuse outcomes to discover treatment-effect heterogeneity, complicating inference after growth and pruning. We develop selective inference for generalized least-squares (GLS) interaction trees with a common covariate basis and known unequal variances. Under a conditional Gaussian model with positive diagonal covariance, weighted orthogonality reduces survival under additive fixed-penalty pruning to one quadratic inequality supplementing the growth event. This yields exact finite-sample conditional tests and confidence intervals, with retained-path and complete-tree inference agreeing on compatible sections. Under causal identification and a correct reference prognosis, the pruning-invariant GLS target is a signed finite-design weighted contrast of conditional average treatment effects. Simulations at $n=100,200,400,800$ and maximum depths one to three search all adjacent-observation midpoints, support calibration and demonstrate over-rejection when pruning survival is omitted. Compared with a 50:50 honest procedure, full-data learning improves reference-split recovery in some small-sample settings. Root-level median intervals can be shorter, while deep-node intervals and upper tails can be much wider; these comparisons concern each procedure’s selected targets. Estimating a common scale with the variance ratio fixed produces modest changes in Selective coverage in the settings examined, without extending the exact guarantee. An exploratory ACTG 175 analysis provides a working-model illustration with estimated arm variances.

Read more

entry.title: Self-Normalized Inference from Riemannian Stochastic Gradient Paths

link.title: Self-Normalized Inference from Riemannian Stochastic Gradient Paths

entry.content:
Riemannian stochastic gradient paths estimate constrained parameters, but confidence regions usually require estimating the Hessian and gradient-noise covariance. We develop self-normalized inference from one path by expressing retained iterates in a common random tangent space. Their average and centered partial sums share an unknown covariance factor that cancels in a Brownian bridge pivot. Under suitable regularity conditions, a joint expansion of the averaged estimator and integrated path controls nonlinear coordinate errors using conditional second moments. The procedure uses fixed-dimensional memory and extends to nondegenerate smooth functionals and alternative local coordinates. Numerical studies show competitive coverage relative to plug-in Wald inference while avoiding Hessian and residual-density estimation.

Read more

entry.title: Sentiment sensing: comparative analysis of multilingual sentiment dynamics

link.title: Sentiment sensing: comparative analysis of multilingual sentiment dynamics

entry.content:
Cross-country sentiment analysis faces three fundamental challenges: language-specific biases distort comparisons, compositional data constraints invalidate standard statistics and temporal dynamics lack rigorous testing frameworks. We introduce sentiment sensing, a framework that addresses these gaps through integrated statistical methods. By combining compositional data analysis, functional data methods, and non-parametric inference, sentiment sensing enables valid multilingual comparisons and statistically defensible detection of sentiment shifts. Our framework has been tested in two case studies, analyzing news articles from the 27 countries of the European Union on the topics of energy and artificial intelligence. Sentiment sensing focuses on multilingual sentiment analysis enabling rigorous comparative science.

Read more

entry.title: Sequentially Doubly Robust Estimation of Conditional Survival Probability with Time-Varying Covariates

link.title: Sequentially Doubly Robust Estimation of Conditional Survival Probability with Time-Varying Covariates

entry.content:
It is often of interest to study the association between covariates and the cumulative incidence of a right-censored time-to-event outcome. When time-varying covariates are measured on a fixed discrete time scale, it is desirable to account for more up-to-date covariates that may inform future censoring. Existing methods rely on stringent parametric assumptions, do not account for informative censoring due to time-varying covariates for continuous time, estimate a marginal survival probability, or do not fully use the discrete-time structure of time-varying covariates. We propose a nonparametric and sequentially doubly robust estimator of the continuous-time survival probability conditional on covariates in this setting. We also show that, in the special case of estimating the marginal survival probability, our estimator is asymptotically efficient. We demonstrate the superior performance of our estimator in a simulation experiment, and apply the method to a COVID-19 vaccine efficacy trial.

Read more

entry.title: Sharp Design-based Inference for Quantiles of Individual Treatment Effects

link.title: Sharp Design-based Inference for Quantiles of Individual Treatment Effects

entry.content:
Understanding the distribution of individual treatment effects (ITEs) is a central problem in causal inference. In general, however, this distribution is only partially identifiable from observed data because it depends on the unidentifiable joint distribution of the two potential outcomes. In this paper, we develop design-based inference for the distribution of ITEs whose validity relies solely on the randomization of treatment assignment, treating the potential outcomes as arbitrary fixed constants. Building on recent randomization tests for ITE quantiles, we propose tests based on either a rank-based Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) statistic or the usual KS statistic, with the latter being more conservative in the presence of ties. We show that, under certain regularity conditions, the confidence bounds obtained by test inversion are asymptotically no worse than the sharp bounds on ITE quantiles given the marginal distributions of the potential outcomes. We further derive a closed-form expression for the confidence bounds from the KS-based randomization test and show that they can be equivalently constructed by combining sharp bounds on ITE quantiles with uncertainty of empirical marginal distributions. This equivalence connects randomization-based inference with partial identification and clarifies the special role of the KS statistic in achieving sharp inference. Under additional distributional assumptions, we characterize the power of the proposed randomization tests under local alternatives. Finally, we discuss how to incorporate covariates to further sharpen inference. We illustrate the properties of the proposed methods using both simulations and a real-data application.

Read more

entry.title: Sharp Generalization for Nonparametric Regression in Interpolation Space by Shallow Over-Parameterized Neural Networks with Channel Attention

link.title: Sharp Generalization for Nonparametric Regression in Interpolation Space by Shallow Over-Parameterized Neural Networks with Channel Attention

entry.content:
We study nonparametric regression using an over-parameterized two-layer ReLU neural network with fixed covariance-based channel attention, trained by gradient descent with both layers updated simultaneously. The spherical covariates follow an arbitrary fixed non-atomic distribution, and the target function lies in an interpolation space with spectral bias widely studied in the statistical learning literature. We prove that early-stopped training achieves regression risk $\cO(\eps_n^2)$, where $\eps_n$ is the critical population rate of the attention kernel $\Kattn$. Its positive eigenvalues are $\lambda_j^{s’}$, where $\lambda_j$ are those of the ReLU feature covariance kernel $K$ and $s’=2s+3$ for $s\ge1$. Under polynomial eigenvalue decay $\lambda_j\asymp j^{-2\alpha}$ with $\alpha>1/2$, the regression risk bound $\cO(\eps_n^2)$ specializes to the minimax optimal rate $\cO(n^{-2\alpha s’/(2\alpha s’+1)})$. Our analysis is based on two new technical results on the optimization and generalization of the attention network. First, the neural network function after every gradient descent iteration admits a decomposition into a function with bounded Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) norm and a uniformly small residual. Second, local Rademacher complexity converts this decomposition into a regression risk bound. Kernel gradient descent on the same ball attains the same rate, while our theorem gives explicit sufficient width and auxiliary-sample conditions for simultaneous network training. Our analysis is further extended to covariates supported on $\RR^d$ through a novel normalization method. Under a sub-Gaussian covariate distribution, the attention network achieves a nearly optimal regression risk $\cO((\log n)n^{-s’(d+3)/(s’(d+3)+d)})$ without a density assumption.

Read more

entry.title: Sharp Partial Identification for Survival Model Comparison Without Target Outcomes

link.title: Sharp Partial Identification for Survival Model Comparison Without Target Outcomes

entry.content:
Hospitals often need to know whether a new prognostic model outperforms an established one before survival outcomes in their own patients are available. Without these outcomes, the performance difference is only partially identified: it lies in an interval whose width reflects how far the target population may depart from the source. We show that this interval should be built for the difference itself, not by bounding each model’s risk separately, because both risks depend on the same unknown outcomes. For the fixed-horizon Brier-risk difference, under bounded shifts in conditional log-odds that may vary in sign and magnitude across patient profiles, we derive the sharp identified set, prove that it is never wider than separate-risk subtraction, characterize exactly when it is narrower, and give a diagnostic, computable without target outcomes, for when a single-shift model narrows the interval only by assuming homogeneity. Censoring-adjusted simultaneous bootstrap envelopes turn these sets into decisions. Across 32 nonzero-sensitivity comparisons in lung cancer, separate-risk bounds were 4.0-11.1 times as wide as direct identified sets, although sampling uncertainty with 35 source deaths prevented directional certification. In a Rotterdam-to-German Breast Cancer Study Group analysis, direct identification supported the candidate model in a comparison that separate subtraction left inconclusive. Hospitals can thus obtain evidence, before local outcomes exist, on whether a candidate model predicts more accurately under explicitly stated population differences.

Read more

entry.title: Six-hourly Probabilistic Precipitation Forecasts Created From Hourly Probabilities

link.title: Six-hourly Probabilistic Precipitation Forecasts Created From Hourly Probabilities

entry.content:
A lightweight neural network is described that produces six-hourly, spatially detailed probabilistic quantitative precipitation forecasts (PQPF) from a sequence of hourly spatially detailed probabilistic forecasts, for lead times from 6 to 72\,h. The hourly forecasts were generated by a ``zero-inflated’’ Attention Residual U-Net that outputs the parameters of a probability distribution including a probability of no precipitation and a weighted mixture of two Gamma distributions at each grid point for each hourly forecast lead time. The six-hourly network passes the six consecutive hourly parameter sets, together with summary statistics of the spatial texture of the raw deterministic forecast, through a small recurrent (GRU) layer and a multi-layer perceptron, and maps them to a corresponding zero-inflated mixture of three Gamma distributions describing the six-hourly accumulated precipitation. Training uses sets of hourly probabilistic forecasts, drawn preferentially from wet and heavy-precipitation cases (importance sampling), and matched Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) six-hourly precipitation accumulations, subject to a quality threshold. The resulting six-hourly probabilistic forecasts are well calibrated and skillful, as demonstrated by reliability diagrams, performance diagrams and Brier Skill Scores evaluated over an out-of-sample period spanning day 12 through the end of every month of 2025. The Brier Skill Scores are consistently and significantly higher than those of a baseline that sums independent draws from the hourly distributions. Forecasts show realistic modulation of precipitation related to terrain variations

entry.title: Sketching in Regression: Sketchy in Practice?

link.title: Sketching in Regression: Sketchy in Practice?

entry.content:
The Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) lemma and its extensions provide tools for solving the $L_2$ regression problem in high-dimensional settings with $n>d$, by transforming a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$, (where $m<n$) while approximately preserving the norms of elements of the subspace. In this paper, we study the theoretical guarantees made by various JL-based subspace embeddings critically and concretely to gauge their practical applicability. We derive concrete versions of results on subspace embeddings in the literature to establish lower bounds on the reduced dimension as well as to concretely analyze the complexity of the Fast JL, OSNAP Transforms among other embeddings. These analyses suggest that guaranteeing substantial computational savings while maintaining the accuracy of the sketched solution requires data dimensions larger than those typically encountered in practice. We also see that, for practically necessary accuracy requirements or for sparsity requirements for computational gain, existing theoretical guarantees lead to substantially large reduced dimensions. This leads to very stringent data requirements for establishing guarantees of any kind.

Read more

entry.title: Soccer: a quantitative analysis of team resilience and the miracle of Bern

link.title: Soccer: a quantitative analysis of team resilience and the miracle of Bern

entry.content:
Resilience is the ability to positively respond to adversity. It has been studied in psychology for several decades, with focus on how individuals overcome traumata or cope with setbacks and obstacles in their professional career. Research on resilience in the sport context is rather new. Activities are based on insights that in highly competitive environments, tiny effects tip the scales. A key question of measuring resilience in sports is what parameters to measure. Here a novel concept is proposed to measure the resilience of soccer teams. The relative frequency of matches is determined, where a soccer team, which is initially trailing by 2 goals, finally succeeds to win the match or at least to reach a draw. The analysis is applied to the last 59 seasons of the German premier soccer league Bundesliga. The empirical data are compared with a theoretical model derived from Poisson distributions. It is shown how leading teams in the premier soccer league differ from the average with respect to resilience, which provides further insights into the hidden secrets of top soccer teams.

Read more

entry.title: Specification-Aware Predictive Uncertainty Decomposition

link.title: Specification-Aware Predictive Uncertainty Decomposition

entry.content:
Classical decompositions of predictive uncertainty, such as the information-theoretic one, are defined for a fixed representation $x$ of the input object. They do not consider that $x$ may be incomplete, nor do they measure how much the missing information can affect the prediction. In Large Language Models, users can clarify an underspecified input without any retraining. The clarified input can describe the user’s unobserved intent $z^*$ more accurately and change the predictive uncertainty about the outcome. In this paper, we formalize this setting probabilistically and derive a three-term decomposition of prediction risk into specification, residual aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainties. We show that at the original information level, when only $x$ is available, the aleatoric uncertainty, represented by a Bayes risk, has two components. The first, which we call specification uncertainty, is the expected reduction in this Bayes risk from revealing the intent. The second is the residual aleatoric uncertainty, i.e., the Bayes risk that remains once the intent is known, averaged over its possible values $z$ given $x$. The distinction is important, as specification uncertainty informs the decision to request clarification before making a prediction. We build approximations of these components and connect them to existing uncertainty measures. Our experiments across different domains and modalities show distinct roles for the three components. Specification uncertainty is the most informative for detecting underspecified inputs, while residual aleatoric uncertainty is the most informative for detecting in-distribution prediction errors.

Read more

The distinction is important, as specification uncertainty informs the decision to request clarification before making a prediction. We build approximations of these components and connect them to existing uncertainty measures. Our experiments across different domains and modalities show distinct roles for the three components. Specification uncertainty is the most informative for detecting underspecified inputs, while residual aleatoric uncertainty is the most informative for detecting in-distribution prediction errors.

entry.title: Specification LASSO and a Flexible Characteristics-Based Asset Pricing Model

link.title: Specification LASSO and a Flexible Characteristics-Based Asset Pricing Model

entry.content:
This paper studies a partially linear semiparametric additive model that allows for interactions among variables in high-dimensional settings. We propose the Specification LASSO (S-LASSO), a two-step method that integrates LASSO and Adaptive Group LASSO to simultaneously perform variable selection and model specification. Theoretically, we establish that S-LASSO possesses oracle properties in terms of selection consistency and asymptotic normality. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that S-LASSO outperforms existing alternatives across a variety of scenarios. Empirically, we apply S-LASSO to a characteristics-based asset pricing model, exploring the linear and nonlinear effects of asset-specific characteristics on cross-sectional returns, as well as their interactions with firm size.

Read more

entry.title: Spectral Degeneration of Self-Attention under Isotropic Score Geometry

link.title: Spectral Degeneration of Self-Attention under Isotropic Score Geometry

entry.content:
We study the spectral structure of the self-attention matrix in Transformer models through an idealized spectral model for the pre-softmax score matrix. Motivated by the rotational isotropy of query and key representations, our model replaces the random token-space orientation of the score matrix by its canonical singular-value representative with a logarithmic spike–bulk separation. Empirical diagnostics on pretrained vision and language transformers motivate this model: token-space singular matrices have nearly uniform eigen-angle distributions, and score spectra are dominated by a small number of effective directions. We then prove that the row-wise softmax map transforms this structure into a degenerate attention matrix: dominant modes are preserved, whereas the bulk spectral distributions concentrate at zero. Stable rank remains bounded for bidirectional attention but grows logarithmically for causal attention. Within the canonical model, these results explain how attention can preserve a small number of dominant directions while compressing the remaining bulk modes.

Read more

entry.title: Spectral Gap Inheritance for Metropolis-Hastings with Reversible Proposals

link.title: Spectral Gap Inheritance for Metropolis-Hastings with Reversible Proposals

entry.content:
We study Metropolis-Hastings kernels whose proposal kernels are reversible with respect to a reference measure, and establish sufficient conditions for such kernels to inherit a nonzero right spectral gap from their proposal kernel. Our conditions require the importance weight of the target relative to the reference measure to be bounded above, but do not require it to be bounded away from zero. Our approach combines a localized Holley-Stroock argument, which yields a local Poincare inequality, with a Lyapunov drift condition. As our main application, we analyze the preconditioned Crank-Nicolson (pCN) algorithm for sampling from measures on a Hilbert space that are absolutely continuous with respect to a Gaussian reference measure. Under local boundedness and quasiconvexity assumptions on the potential, we establish a dimension-independent $L^2$-spectral gap for this Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, thereby covering cases in which the local Lipschitz condition used by Hairer et al. (2014) is not satisfied.

Read more

entry.title: Spectrally Tuned Bandwidth Selection for Kernel Fuzzy Relational Clustering

link.title: Spectrally Tuned Bandwidth Selection for Kernel Fuzzy Relational Clustering

entry.content:
Fuzzy clustering is used to identify overlapping geometric cluster structures through partial memberships. However, classical methods are limited by the assumption of equal variable importance and by sensitivity to the fuzzifier parameter. These limitations may yield equal cluster membership probabilities, which we refer to as the uniform solution. To address these issues, we propose Kernel Fuzzy Relational Clustering (KFRC) equipped with a bandwidth selection algorithm tuned via the spectral properties of the induced kernel Gram matrix. The KFRC framework implicitly performs unsupervised kernel metric learning by controlling the geometric embedding of the data through adjustable bandwidth parameters. We conduct a formal stability analysis to identify the exact theoretical conditions under which relational clustering collapses, thereby ensuring the stable performance of KFRC. We find that our two-stage bandwidth selection procedure adapts to the data structure while actively avoiding the uniform solution. Furthermore, this theoretical analysis leads to the proposal of a novel fuzzifier function that presents distinct advantages over the power fuzzifier function. We conduct experiments on several synthetic and publicly available data sets to demonstrate that the proposed framework recovers complex structures that traditional methods fail to resolve, while avoiding both uniform and near-crisp solutions.

Read more

entry.title: Stage-wise semiparametric analysis of multivariate event times under informative censoring via vine copula

link.title: Stage-wise semiparametric analysis of multivariate event times under informative censoring via vine copula

entry.content:
The analysis of times to multiple nonterminal events arises in many lifetime data settings, where the nonterminal event times are subject to informative censoring by a terminal event, posing substantial challenges. We propose a likelihood-based regression framework that models dependence among multiple nonterminal and terminal event times using a vine copula. This framework allows pairwise associations between nonterminal and terminal events, as well as among nonterminal events, to vary across event types, while enabling valid regression inference for the marginal distributions of individual event times. To facilitate computation, we develop a stage-wise pseudo-likelihood estimation procedure and establish its large-sample properties. We demonstrate satisfactory finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators and associated variance estimators through simulation studies. We also illustrate the proposed methodology using data from a crowdfunding platform to examine the relationship between different types of creator-backer interactions and a creator’s lifetime on the platform.

Read more

entry.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions

link.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions

entry.content:
Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle’s rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.

Read more

entry.title: Statistical Inference under Performativity: From Policy Feedback to Self-Evolving Systems

link.title: Statistical Inference under Performativity: From Policy Feedback to Self-Evolving Systems

entry.content:
Performativity arises when prediction-informed decisions change the data-generating process, creating feedback between deployment and learning. This phenomenon occurs in policy-making and in self-evolving AI systems that shape their own future training data. Statistical inference is challenging because estimation errors in earlier predictors affect subsequent data distributions and propagate into later updates. We develop an end-to-end framework for statistical inference under performativity. For repeated risk minimization and repeated gradient descent, we establish central limit theorems at fixed deployment rounds and derive covariance recursions that capture both current-round sampling variation and uncertainty inherited from earlier deployments. We develop consistent covariance estimators using policy perturbations and score matching. These results can yield asymptotically valid confidence regions for population iterates and the performative stable point. We further extend prediction-powered inference to this dynamic setting, combining labeled observations with predictions on additional unlabeled data to improve statistical efficiency. We evaluate our framework in synthetic, semi-synthetic educational, and self-evolving large language model routing settings. Our experiments demonstrate that ignoring propagated uncertainty can lead to substantial undercoverage even after repeated retraining. Together, these results provide statistical tools for learning systems that help determine the distributions from which they learn. Our work establish a complete statistical inference under performativity, introducing new challenges and inference settings that we believe will provide substantial value to policy-making, statistics, and machine learning.

Read more

entry.title: Statistical Machine Learning for Astronomy – A Textbook

link.title: Statistical Machine Learning for Astronomy – A Textbook

entry.content:
This textbook gives a systematic treatment of statistical machine learning for astronomical research, based on Bayesian inference. It shows how modern data analysis techniques connect to classical statistical methods and follow from familiar statistical principles. The Bayesian perspective, used throughout, gives priority to uncertainty quantification and statistical rigor, which scientific inference in astronomy needs. The textbook progresses from probability theory and Bayesian inference through supervised learning, including linear regression with measurement uncertainties, logistic regression and classification. Unsupervised learning topics cover Principal Component Analysis and clustering methods. We then introduce sampling and Markov Chain Monte Carlo, followed by Gaussian Processes as probabilistic nonparametric methods and neural networks in the broader statistical context. Our theory-focused approach derives each method from first principles with complete mathematical development and then shows its astronomical applications. We put statistical insight first and explain why algorithms work, when they are appropriate, and how they connect to broader statistical principles. From a solid grounding in classical methods and their theory, the treatment leads to modern techniques such as neural networks. With this grounding, readers can apply the methods to astronomical research with proper attention to assumptions, limits and uncertainty propagation, as large astronomical surveys require. The 22 companion tutorials apply the methods to astronomical data in Jupyter notebooks.

Read more

entry.title: Statistical Sheaf Modeling Methods for Measuring Qualia Structures

link.title: Statistical Sheaf Modeling Methods for Measuring Qualia Structures

entry.content:
Mathematical sheaves are an abstraction that captures the notion that consistency between local properties can lead to a global picture. There are a number of (mathematical) phenomena that sheaves exhibit, which seem tantalizingly close to what one might hope a theory of qualia would explain. Recently, the theory and abstraction of sheaves has been transformed into robust computational tools for understanding complex systems. These tools are now ripe to help qualia researchers forge robust and testable models. Intuitively, as conscious entities, rather than experiencing ``everything all at once,’’ our experience is coherent to varying degrees. Sheaves can model this rather nicely. This chapter presents the practical and theoretical considerations of sheaves in data modeling, with a view towards computational models that can support statistical hypothesis testing.

Read more

entry.title: Stochastic optimization methods through statistical whitening

link.title: Stochastic optimization methods through statistical whitening

entry.content:
We provide new statistical insights into designing stochastic optimization methods. By modeling the gradient via a normal distribution, we argue that the stochastic gradient should be whitened using its covariance. We give an online method for estimating the mean and variance of the gradients based on regularized likelihood or, equivalently, through a maximum a posteriori estimate. We then show how to use structured approximations to the covariance within this same framework, which includes diagonal and Kronecker-factored approximations. The diagonal approximation results in a method that is very closely related to Adam and performs as well in practice. The Kronecker approximation results in the new MN method, which is a variant of Shampoo and KL-Shampoo. We also recover Muon by applying this same statistical framework to the gradient direction rather than the full gradient. By combining this with a whitening step, we arrive at MN-Muon, a novel preconditioned version of Muon. Our experiments on GPT-2-type models at Chinchilla scale indicate that MND, the diagonal implementation of MN, outperforms both the Distributed Shampoo and the KL-Shampoo implementations in terms of stability, final validation loss and time taken. MND-Muon, the diagonal implementation of MN-Muon, improves on Muon in 21 of 24 paired GPT-small runs and achieves a lower best validation loss on GPT-medium, where it remains stable over the six tested learning rates. However, we found that NorMuon was comparable to MND-Muon and achieved a slightly lower validation loss on GPT-medium and at GPT-small batch 512 on FineWeb.

Read more

entry.title: Strictly proper scoring rules for node selection tasks on graphs

link.title: Strictly proper scoring rules for node selection tasks on graphs

entry.content:
In node selection tasks, the goal is to identify a single unknown target node in a graph. We consider probabilistic supervised node selection, where the estimator outputs a probability distribution over the nodes of the graph and the ground-truth node is available for evaluation. Classical evaluation metrics for such tasks are either statistically ill-conceived or blind to the graph structure. To fill this gap, we introduce two strictly proper scoring rules that are explicitly graph-aware: the Resistance score, which is parameter-free, and the Diffusion score, which operates at an adjustable coarse-graining resolution. We show that the Diffusion score interpolates between the multi-category Brier score and a cluster-level weighted Brier score. The Resistance score generalises two classical scoring rules: the multi-category Brier score and the Ranked probability score. Applied to rooted trees, it also serves as the strictly proper version of the improper Hierarchical error distance used in hierarchical classification. In the same setting, we furthermore establish strict propriety of the Hierarchical cross-entropy family, a recently introduced separate class of hierarchy-aware scoring rules. Experiments on epidemic source detection and on ImageNet classification confirm that the proposed scores detect meaningful differences in estimation quality that classical metrics miss.

Read more

entry.title: Studentized inference in randomized experiments when a few units dominate the outcome variation

link.title: Studentized inference in randomized experiments when a few units dominate the outcome variation

entry.content:
In completely randomized experiments with heavy-tailed outcomes, a few units can carry a share of the residual variation that does not vanish as the number of units grows. We study the studentized difference in means and Lin’s regression-adjusted estimator, with covariates whose leverage vanishes, when the finite population is fixed, and the treatment assignment is the only source of randomness. The studentized statistic then has a nonnormal limit in general. Populations with the same marginal distributions of potential outcomes can have different limits, as the limit depends on the unobserved pairing mechanism of the two potential outcomes of each dominant unit. When the outcome errors are drawn from a heavy-tailed law, the limit is random and, outside a degenerate case, varies with the population. Under balanced allocation, the conventional Wald interval has an explicit asymptotic coverage floor. At the nominal level $0.95$, the floor is about $0.42$ for every population and about $0.84$ when the two potential residuals of each unit are equal. Both floors are close to the best possible, and without balanced allocation, the coverage can fall to the smaller of the proportions of treated and control units.

Read more

entry.title: Subgradient Methods for Nonsmooth Sample Average Approximation

link.title: Subgradient Methods for Nonsmooth Sample Average Approximation

entry.content:
We study direct subgradient methods for nonsmooth sample average approximation (SAA). Subgradient descent and Nesterov acceleration with constant step sizes attain polynomial and geometric rates matching their smooth counterparts. After $O(\log n)$ full-batch updates, where $n$ is the sample size, the computed solution has the same first-order expansion and limiting distribution as an SAA solution, even when the iterates do not converge. A bound on subgradient increments transfers population regularity to the sample objective, controls the algorithmic trajectory, and identifies the leading random term. The bound covers convex piecewise linear scenario costs, including two-stage stochastic linear programs with fixed recourse. Moreau smoothing displaces the population solution at first order and changes the limiting distribution of the computed solution. An explicit shift of the residual removes the first-order displacement and improves the expansion remainder. For sparse decisions, restricted increment bounds give convergence, support recovery, and expansions for proximal subgradient descent and iterative hard thresholding.

Read more

entry.title: Subpolynomial-Query Proximal Sampling Beyond Log-Concavity

link.title: Subpolynomial-Query Proximal Sampling Beyond Log-Concavity

entry.content:
We study the gradient query complexity of sampling from a density $\pi(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ has a $ eta$-Lipschitz gradient but need not be convex. Our approach uses the proximal sampler, which alternates Gaussian perturbation with sampling a position conditional on the noisy observation. We implement its observation chain using the high-order noisy conditional sampler of [OpenAI 2026], obtaining improved dimension dependence under functional inequalities. If $\pi$ satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality (LSI) with constant $\alpha$, then for every fixed $ u>0$, there is a finite constant $C_ u$ depending only on $ u$ such that the algorithm returns a sample within total-variation distance $\varepsilon$ using at most $C_ u\kappa(d+\kappa+\varepsilon^{-1}+| abla V(x_0)|^2/ eta)^ u$ queries, where $\kappa= eta/\alpha$ and $x_0$ is an arbitrary reference point for initialization. The analysis controls center-dependent local errors along exact proximal histories and removes the final observation noise by conditional decoding. Under a Poincar'e inequality (PI), we obtain a corresponding guarantee from a warm start with a known bound on its R'enyi divergence. An oracle lower bound shows that a stationary point alone, which suffices under LSI, is insufficient under PI.

u$ queries, where $\kappa= eta/\alpha$ and $x_0$ is an arbitrary reference point for initialization. entry.title: Surrogate Losses for Fairness-Aware Classification: Fisher Consistency and Calibration

link.title: Surrogate Losses for Fairness-Aware Classification: Fisher Consistency and Calibration

entry.content:
Fairness-aware classification seeks to balance predictive accuracy and fairness across demographic groups. Although surrogate losses facilitate the optimization of fairness-aware objectives, it remains unclear when minimizing these losses yields optimal decisions under the original fairness-aware risk. This paper investigates the statistical validity of surrogate-based fairness-aware classification under demographic parity and equal opportunity, considering both attribute-blind and attribute-aware settings. We introduce fairness-aware Fisher consistency and characterize it through conditions on the derivatives of the surrogate losses. The characterization shows that consistency depends not only on the individual loss functions but also on their interaction within the fairness-regularized objective. We further establish a calibration inequality that relates the excess fairness-aware risk to the excess surrogate risk, providing a quantitative connection between surrogate optimization and the original classification objective. Numerical experiments illustrate how deviations from the consistency conditions affect fairness-aware excess risk and how the regularization parameter influences the well-posedness of surrogate optimization. An application to consumer credit default prediction demonstrates that appropriately calibrated fairness regularization can substantially reduce demographic disparities while maintaining predictive performance.

Read more

entry.title: Surrogate Modeling and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Complex Systems: A Workflow for Automated Simulation Exploration

link.title: Surrogate Modeling and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Complex Systems: A Workflow for Automated Simulation Exploration

entry.content:
Complex systems are increasingly explored through simulation-driven workflows that combine physics-based and empirical models with optimization and analytics. Despite their power, these workflows face two central obstacles: high computational cost from repeated expensive simulator runs, and limited transparency when decisions rely on opaque black-box models. We propose a workflow that addresses both challenges by training lightweight emulators on compact designs of experiments that (i) provide fast, low-latency approximations of expensive simulators, (ii) enable rigorous uncertainty quantification, and (iii) support global and local eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) analyses. This work formalizes a methodological bridge accommodating continuous, categorical, and integer variables across diverse domains, from engineering design to socio-environmental agent-based models. To validate surrogate explanations and examine how faithfully they reflect simulator behavior, we introduce a comparative methodology incorporating active validation filters, including explanation consistency and aleatoric uncertainty quantification. Furthermore, we provide practical guidelines for coupling experimental designs with emulator training to select architectures that balance computational efficiency with interpretability. We demonstrate the framework across two contrasting paradigms: a deterministic multidisciplinary design simulation of a hybrid-electric aircraft and a stochastic agent-based simulation of urban segregation. Results show that coupling surrogates with XAI enables large-scale exploration in seconds, reveals critical nonlinear interactions, and highlights potential design and policy levers while establishing consistent explanations across architectures.

Read more

entry.title: SynForecast: Controlled Synthetic Time Series for Forecasting Research

link.title: SynForecast: Controlled Synthetic Time Series for Forecasting Research

entry.content:
Synthetic time series constitute a substantial share of the training corpora of several recent forecasting foundation models. Existing studies report benefits at small data budgets and modest synthetic proportions, but each evaluates individual combinations of model and generator. Studying these benefits systematically requires generators that support controlled configuration, perturbation, reproducibility and mechanism-level ablation, and the 11 existing generators we review show gaps in this combined support. We present SynForecast, an open-source Python library with 32 generators, 19 of which implement named mechanisms with a published source in econometrics, quantitative finance, statistical physics and point-process theory. Perturbations and mechanism families can be varied while everything else is held fixed, output comes in the long format that forecasting libraries accept, and output does not depend on the number of parallel workers. We evaluate SynForecast on M4 at five frequencies with a neural network and a gradient-boosted ensemble. A classical baseline attains the lowest error in nine of ten frequency-history combinations. A synthetic prior outperforms the same network trained from scratch at a fixed budget by up to 34% with a few dozen observations, but loses to it at full history at every frequency, and none of three pre-specified rescalings of history predicts where the sign changes. At the hourly frequency, where the prior fails at every history, the corpus lacks daily cycles; adding them reduces zero-shot error by 43 to 63% for both models. Fine-tuning outperforms training from scratch by up to about 15%, but at short histories a fixed 300-step fine-tune is worse than the pretrained model used as is. Removing the classical mechanism family costs about 2% for both models; every other family has a smaller effect outside the hourly frequency.

entry.title: Tail persistence of extremes at finite and asymptotic levels with Bayesian hierarchical inference

link.title: Tail persistence of extremes at finite and asymptotic levels with Bayesian hierarchical inference

entry.content:
Tail persistence characterizes the relative escalation of observations beyond an extreme threshold and complements conventional summaries such as return levels and tail indices. Existing literature is mainly distribution-based and does not account for uncertainty, nonstationarity, or covariate effects. We develop a Bayesian framework for modeling tail persistence under generalized extreme value and generalized Pareto models. We first make explicit the connection between tail persistence and the extreme value index under regular variation, which identifies the asymptotic persistence with $1/(1-\xi)$ and links persistence to tail heaviness. We then derive closed-form expressions for persistence at finite quantile levels under both models and show that, for any location–scale extreme value family with a common shape parameter, finite-level persistence depends on the location and scale parameters only through their ratio. Motivated by these results and by the weak identifiability of observation-specific shape parameters, we formulate a Bayesian hierarchical extreme value model in which the shape parameter is constant over time, while the location and scale parameters vary with covariates and latent effects. The asymptotic persistence is then a single, well-identified quantity, whereas finite-level persistence evolves over time through the location–scale structure. The framework provides posterior inference for both quantities, with credible intervals and probabilistic assessment of temporal evolution and covariate effects. Through simulation studies and real-data applications, we show that persistence provides an interpretable characterization of the escalation of extremes beyond high thresholds, complementing classical extreme value summaries with comprehensive uncertainty quantification in nonstationary settings. The methodology is implemented in an open-source \texttt{R} package.

entry.title: TempoPFN: Synthetic Pre-training of Linear RNNs for Zero-shot Time Series Forecasting

link.title: TempoPFN: Synthetic Pre-training of Linear RNNs for Zero-shot Time Series Forecasting

entry.content:
Foundation models for zero-shot time series forecasting face challenges in efficient long-horizon prediction and reproducibility, with existing synthetic-only approaches underperforming on challenging benchmarks. This paper presents TempoPFN, a univariate time series foundation model based on linear Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) pre-trained exclusively on synthetic data. The model uses a GatedDeltaProduct architecture with state-weaving for fully parallelizable training across sequence lengths, eliminating the need for windowing or summarization techniques while maintaining robust temporal state-tracking. Our comprehensive synthetic data pipeline unifies diverse generators, including stochastic differential equations, Gaussian processes, and audio synthesis, with novel augmentations. In zero-shot evaluations on the Gift-Eval, fev-bench and Chronos-ZS benchmarks, TempoPFN achieves top-tier competitive performance, surpassing the majority of models trained on real-world data, while leveraging fully parallelizable training and inference. We open-source our complete data generation pipeline and training code, providing a reproducible foundation for future research.

entry.title: Temporal Seam Score for Assessing Continuity at Known Transitions in Time Series

link.title: Temporal Seam Score for Assessing Continuity at Known Transitions in Time Series

entry.content:
Long environmental records increasingly combine observations from successive observing or processing systems. Transitions between these systems create temporal seams that may reflect imperfect harmonization or changes in the observed process. We introduce the Temporal Seam Score (S-score, or S), a signed, robust measure for assessing continuity at a known transition time. The complete time series is fitted with a seam-blind model accounting for trend, seasonality, and optional covariates. The residual contrast between symmetric windows around the transition is compared with matched reference contrasts calculated within the contributing segments. The S-score is the standardized departure of the seam contrast from this reference. An S-score near zero indicates that the seam is consistent with ordinary temporal variability. Its sign indicates the direction of the discontinuity, while its magnitude ( S ) indicates how exceptional the discontinuity is. Simulation showed that S reflects the imposed discontinuity relative to residual variability: a 20% shift produced a median S of 2.58 at a residual coefficient of variation of 0.10, compared with 0.84 at 0.50. In a MODIS-to-Sentinel-3 vegetation record, 121 of 500 sites yielded finite S-scores, of which 90 met all reliability criteria. Among these reliable sites, median S was +0.217 and median S was 0.627, indicating little systematic directional displacement and a median seam departure below one reference spread. The S-score provides a general and auditable diagnostic for evaluating temporal continuity across generations of sensors, algorithms, and observing systems without requiring temporal overlap, thereby supporting harmonization quality assurance and more reliable attribution analyses based on long-term environmental records.

Read more

entry.title: Testable and Actionable Calibration for Full Swap Regret

link.title: Testable and Actionable Calibration for Full Swap Regret

entry.content:
AI generated predictions increasingly inform decision making in critical tasks, and therefore must be trustworthy. One widely used measure of trustworthiness is calibration, which requires that the predictions match the true frequencies and can be treated like real probabilities of a given outcome. However, defining calibration is subtle, and designing good measures of calibration error has been an active topic of recent research. The first goal is to find calibration measures that are actionable, meaning they can inform decision makers about their utility loss when predictions are treated as true probabilities, which is known as swap regret. The second goal is to find calibration measures that are testable, meaning that calibration error can be measured from a small sample of predictions and outcomes. Although these are very basic requirements, there is no existing calibration measure that fully satisfies both properties, and all existing measures relax actionability by bounding a weaker notion of swap regret, or relax testability by having suboptimal estimation error. We introduce a new calibration measure, Soft-Binned Calibration Decision Loss (SCDL), which we prove is fully actionable without weakening either requirement, and testable with nearly optimal error rate. In addition, SCDL satisfies other desired properties such as continuity and consistency. We also provide a set of experiments confirming that the theoretical advantages of SCDL compared to other measures lead to better performance in practice.

entry.title: The Hardness of Estimating Cross-Entropy Risk for Language Models

link.title: The Hardness of Estimating Cross-Entropy Risk for Language Models

entry.content:
Language models, once pretrained, are routinely assessed by the holdout method, which estimates their per-token cross-entropy risk—a quantity that may be finite or infinite. We prove possibility and impossibility theorems that characterize the hardness of this estimation problem. The estimand depends on two objects: the unknown data distribution $p$ and the distribution $q$ induced by the language model under study. Our ignorance of $p$ is empirical, whereas our ignorance of $q$, or at least of its tail, is mathematical; so the parameter space {\em should} range over pairs $(p,q)$—a product space—to fully capture our ignorance. {\em Negative results}: no estimator is pointwise consistent, even when the parameter space is restricted to full-support models and to data distributions whose expected text length is below a fixed bound; worse, every estimator fails on a dense set of pairs. {\em Positive results}: the holdout estimator becomes pointwise consistent when the models are further restricted to Transformers or, architecture-neutrally, to full-support models with a finite context window; and, where no such design is in place, it still consistently estimates the risk capped at any fixed threshold, which suffices for screening candidate models in practice. {\em Lesson}: designs such as the Transformer architecture and finite context windows, although adopted for computational or engineering reasons, pay a {\em statistical dividend}: they suffice to make pointwise consistency possible—a dividend visible only in how they turn a negative result into positive ones.

Read more

entry.title: The Prior-Force Family of Implicit Denoiser Priors and Its Decisions in Linear Inverse Problems

link.title: The Prior-Force Family of Implicit Denoiser Priors and Its Decisions in Linear Inverse Problems

entry.content:
Implicit priors given by Gaussian denoisers successfully regularize a wide range of inverse problems in approaches such as plug-and-play (PnP), regularization by denoising (RED) and score-based methods. Such a prior depends on the noise level, and how it selects among signals consistent with the data remains largely uncharacterized. To put implicit and explicit priors on the same footing, we define the prior-force family $W_t=t^{-1}(D_t^{-1}-I)$ of any Gaussian denoiser $D_t$ at noise variance $t>0$ (inverse in the graph sense), the normalized denoising residual as an operator on clean signals. At a common effective prior weight, the equilibrium equations differ only in their prior terms: PnP uses $W_t$, RED/score-based methods the score force (the normalized residual as an operator on noisy inputs), and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation the MAP force (the negative log-prior gradient). For the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) denoisers of a prior $\pi$, we compare the corresponding energies at three levels. Without observation, raising the noise level favors PnP minima that retain more posterior variance. On signals consistent with the data, the leading-order PnP energy for separated modes is the proximal hull of the MAP energy, which lets PnP select signals between modes; modes of equal data fit are ranked by peak height at small noise levels and by mass at large ones. For recovery, $W_t$ at the truth bounds the local bias, and an oracle noise level balances this bias against denoiser error. These results show that the noise level is a parameter of the prior rather than a step size. Experiments with exact priors support these predictions, including the mixture components that PnP selects on unseen data.

entry.title: The Root Finding Problem Revisited: Beyond the Robbins-Monro procedure

link.title: The Root Finding Problem Revisited: Beyond the Robbins-Monro procedure

entry.content:
We study the sequential root-finding problem with repeated noisy measurements. We propose sequential-test bisection STB, which uses a nonparametric sequential sign test to determine when to move to a new design point. Compared with variants of stochastic approximation, STB offers broader adaptivity and faster convergence. When the regression function satisfies $ f(x) \geq \textsf{c}_0 x-\theta ^\gamma$ in a neighborhood of $\theta$ for constants $\textsf{c}_0,\gamma>0$ where $\theta$ is the root, i.e. $f(\theta) = 0$, we establish non-asymptotic guarantees showing that STB, without using the knowledge of $\gamma$, achieves the minimax adaptive optimal convergence rate $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/(2\gamma)})$, outperforming Robbins–Monro and related stochastic-approximation methods in convergence rate. Under sub-Gaussian noise, STB provides finite-sample confidence sequences for the root $\theta$ without estimating a derivative. In the positive-slope model, we augment STB with {randomized weighted-section and a line fitted to all observations}, leading to asymptotic normality and consistent variance estimation. We formalize the efficiency by a convolution theorem of H'ajek-Le Cam type. Furthermore, when the regression function is discontinuous at the root, we show that Robbins–Monro converges at rate $1/n$, whereas STB converges super-polynomially. We extend this construction to multivariate nonparametric level-set estimation by sampling along rays. As a technical byproduct, we establish a new central limit theorem under random stopping, with proof techniques that may be of independent interest.

entry.title: The Staged Pandora’s Box: Reservation Indices for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization

link.title: The Staged Pandora’s Box: Reservation Indices for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization

entry.content:
A staged search must decide which candidate to advance next and when to stop. Some observations only inform later decisions; others can be kept as results. We formulate these choices as a staged Pandora’s box with a designated set of collectable stages. For independent finite-stage candidates with bounded readings and positive bounded own-history costs, an exact covered-call recursion gives the reservation index, the optimal value and the loss of every advance or stop; advancing an index-maximal candidate while its index exceeds the incumbent is optimal. The representation recovers classical single-stage search, nested inspection and the all-collectable Markov setting, and prices changes in the problem: enlarging the collectable set or lowering costs raises the value by an explicit covered-call overshoot. Resumption can be valuable even when future reward laws do not change, but has no value for deterministic readings. With information sharing across candidates, no rule using only their separate remaining-reading laws is universally optimal, and making an intermediate reading collectable can change which candidate is inspected first. Under a coherent joint path law with own-history costs, an approximate-planning bound controls the recomputed index’s regret by changes in untouched candidates’ local values; a common-component specialization bounds those changes through predictive total-variation dispersion. Exact finite-law experiments check the representation, the loss accounting and the bounds.

Exact finite-law experiments check the representation, the loss accounting and the bounds.

entry.title: The Statistical Geometry of Latent Recovery in Hidden Markov Models

link.title: The Statistical Geometry of Latent Recovery in Hidden Markov Models

entry.content:
Hidden Markov models (HMMs) offer an important capability to interpret fitted latent states and transitions. When emission distributions nearly coincide, a small observation-density error does not ensure accurate estimation of the latent quantities needed for interpretation. This motivates us to characterize convergence rates for latent recovery that account for emission separation. Our main contribution lies in deriving deterministic inverse inequalities that convert Hellinger error between fitted and true densities into bounds on latent recovery errors. We develop these bounds for multivariate Gaussian HMMs with a common, known emission covariance matrix and combine them with a Hellinger estimation guarantee for the global maximum likelihood estimator to obtain latent recovery rates. Although the joint observation distribution is a Gaussian mixture with exponentially many path components, they share the same emission centers across time. Leveraging this shared structure, we show that the separation exponents are governed by the maximum number of simultaneously approaching centers rather than the number of path components. Under exact specification, the global bounds on state-sequence probability discrepancies and the 1-Wasserstein loss for latent location distributions exhibit sharp separation exponents that do not increase with the number of selected times. Moreover, sufficiently small observation-density error guarantees unique matching between fitted and true emission centers, which yields error bounds for individual emission centers and transition rows. Under over-specification, individual split-state transition rows are not necessarily identifiable, so we quantify aggregate latent recovery errors and show that state-sequence probability bounds incur larger separation exponents compared to exact specification. We conduct synthetic experiments to validate our theoretical results.

entry.title: Theoretical Guarantees for the Subspace-Constrained Tyler’s Estimator

link.title: Theoretical Guarantees for the Subspace-Constrained Tyler’s Estimator

entry.content:
We study the subspace-constrained Tyler’s estimator (STE) for recovering a low-dimensional linear subspace from data contaminated by outliers. Under deterministic conditions on inlier spread and outlier alignment, we prove linear convergence to the true subspace from a sufficiently accurate initialization. The guarantee also applies when the dimension-scaled signal-to-noise ratio is below one, where general robust subspace recovery is SSE-hard. When initializing STE from a candidate subspace, we provide a sufficient recovery condition based on the initial angular error and the size of the identity shift applied to the subspace projector. For noisy inliers, we prove a subspace error proportional to the noise level within an explicit iteration bound. Finally, under an asymptotic, anisotropic Gaussian inlier–outlier model, we show that Tyler’s M-estimator (TME) provides a successful STE initialization even when TME’s own leading eigenspace differs from the target subspace.

entry.title: Theoretical guidelines for annealed Langevin dynamics in compositional simulation-based inference

link.title: Theoretical guidelines for annealed Langevin dynamics in compositional simulation-based inference

entry.content:
Compositional score-based approaches to simulation-based inference (SBI) approximate the posterior over a shared parameter given $n$ independent observations by aggregating individually learned posterior scores: currently, there are two main propositions of such methods (Geffner et al. (2023), Linhart et al. (2026)). As the resulting composite score does not correspond to the score of any distribution along the forward diffusion path of the true multi-observation posterior, sampling from it via a reverse SDE leads to an irreducible bias. Annealed Langevin dynamics provides a principled alternative: it treats the composite score as the genuine score of a sequence of tractable bridging densities and samples from them in succession. When properly tuned, it could lead to a controllable bias. However, its hyperparameters, namely step sizes, the number of steps per level, and the number of annealing levels, have so far been chosen empirically. We derive Wasserstein bounds for annealed Langevin with approximate scores and translate them into explicit decision rules for these hyperparameters that guarantee a prescribed sampling accuracy, while highlighting different theoretical aspects of each composite score formulation. In the Gaussian setting, we obtain closed-form expressions for all relevant quantities and prove that the bridging densities of Linhart et al. (2026) consistently admit larger step sizes and require fewer total Langevin steps than those of Geffner et al. (2023). Furthermore, we show empirically that the tuning obtained in the Gaussian setting generalizes to more complex problems, thus providing a well-understood and theoretically grounded starting point for practitioners using compositional score-based approaches.

Read more

entry.title: The precision of fractional factorial designs under randomization

link.title: The precision of fractional factorial designs under randomization

entry.content:
A regular fraction of a two-level factorial design runs fewer treatment combinations (cells), with more units in each. With the number of units fixed, more units per cell do not by themselves reduce the variance. Averaged over the fractions of one defining contrast subgroup, a fraction’s variance is smaller than the full design’s by the unit-to-unit variation of the aliased effects, a gain the usual variance estimator misses. Assuming the aliased effects are zero, we propose a full-design estimator that weights the fractions’ contrasts by inverse variance. Its estimated variance never exceeds the saturated estimator’s. In large samples, it is proportional to the harmonic mean of the fractions’ average cell variances, and a fraction’s, on average, to the arithmetic mean. We test this assumption, but choosing between the two estimators by the test can lose coverage. The results extend to unequal allocations, and the large-sample results to covariate adjustment.

Read more

entry.title: Tight Stochastic Sequential Covers for General VC Classes with Unknown i.i.d. Features

link.title: Tight Stochastic Sequential Covers for General VC Classes with Unknown i.i.d. Features

entry.content:
We study hybrid online learning with stochastic features and adversarial labels when the feature distribution is unknown. Prior work gave stochastic sequential covers of log-size $O(d\log^2 T)$ for a general VC class and logarithmic bounds only under stronger star-type structure. We show that finite VC dimension alone is enough: every binary class of VC dimension $d$ admits a distribution-blind exact cover with log-size $O(d\log T+\log(1/\delta))$, matching the worst-case $\Omega(d\log(T/d))$ dependence on the horizon. The key ingredient is a new local cube weight that counts Boolean subcubes incident to each realizable trace. Unlike the equal splits used in earlier constructions, we split mass unevenly according to these cube weights; a coordinate-deletion inequality shows that VC dimension controls the total cost of these splits. This yields, to our knowledge, the first tight $O((d+1)\log T)$ expected worst-case log-loss regret for general VC partitions with unknown i.i.d. features, and an exact polynomial-time implementation for planar affine halfspaces. We also show that the binary phenomenon does not extend from VC dimension to pseudo-dimension: a fixed pseudo-dimension-one sigmoid class requires $\Omega(\log^2 T)$ bits for uniform sequential approximation at accuracy $1/T$.

entry.title: Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation

link.title: Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation

entry.content:
Convexity has three equivalent descriptions: support by affine functions, monotonicity of the subdifferential, and increasing secant slopes. We weaken all three by one distortion with parameter $\gamma\in(0,1]$, which multiplies positive changes by $\gamma$ and divides negative ones by $\gamma$. The resulting classes are the convex functions at $\gamma=1$ and, for $\gamma<1$, are distinct and nested, with the parameter dropping by at most a square along the chain. For proper lower semicontinuous functions in these classes, the effective domain is convex, local minimizers are global, and the function is locally Lipschitz on the relative interior of its domain. The classes separate offline from online optimization over compact convex sets with efficient projection, with access to function values and bounded support vectors. A smooth member of any class can be minimized to additive accuracy $\varepsilon$ with $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ first-order queries and projections. Online, with nonpositive losses and $\alpha$-regret measured against $\alpha$ times the best fixed point, a polynomial-time algorithm achieves $\gamma$-regret $O(\sqrt T)$ on the largest class. For every fixed, effectively specified $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and every $\alpha\in(\gamma,1]$, no randomized polynomial-time algorithm has sublinear expected $\alpha$-regret unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, already for smooth concave polynomial losses in the smallest class, each minimized by one linear optimization. Thus, unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, $\gamma$ is the exact online coefficient of each class, while the offline coefficient is one.

Read more

entry.title: Time Partitioning in Target Trial Emulation

link.title: Time Partitioning in Target Trial Emulation

entry.content:
In target trial emulation, the treatment strategies that patients follow are inferred from the treatments they actually receive in routine care. However, in most settings, the outcome may preclude the observation of planned treatment, giving rise to immortal time bias through misclassification of treatment strategy, while markers of treatment response may influence subsequent treatment decisions, giving rise to time-varying confounding. A key step toward unbiased treatment effect estimation is to partition follow-up into sufficiently short time intervals to unfold the feedback relationships involving treatment and represent the resulting causal relations with a directed acyclic graph. In this study, we present the possible within-interval causal orderings induced by this partitioning, discuss their causal implications, and assess their plausibility across clinical settings. For each causal ordering, we derive the corresponding g-formula. Using ancestral multi-world networks and simulations, we show that the standard cloning-censoring-weighting estimator is invalid when treatment affects the outcome within a time interval, and we propose a modified version of the method that restores its validity in this setting. Finally, we analyze the consequences of choosing time intervals that are either excessively wide or excessively narrow, thereby formally establishing the need for time partitioning and providing practical guidance for selecting an appropriate partition based on the clinical setting.

Read more

entry.title: Time-Specific Multinomial Logistic Regression for Competing Risks

link.title: Time-Specific Multinomial Logistic Regression for Competing Risks

entry.content:
Motivated by the project on premature menopause among childhood cancer survivors in the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study (CCSS), we develop methods for estimating time-specific factor effects using doubly censored event time data with competing risks. We begin with fitting separate binary logistic regression models for different causes. However, the approach does not ensure the sum of the resulting estimated cumulative incidence rates remains bounded by one. To overcome this limitation, we consider a multinomial logistic regression formulation to jointly model all cause-specific risks. Two inverse-probability-of-censoring-weight (IPCW) based estimating functions are proposed accordingly. To handle the estimation instability caused by data separation, we incorporate the Firth-type penalization in those estimating functions to obtain more stable coefficient estimators. The sandwich variance estimator is applied to estimate the standard errors. A weighted quasi-likelihood information criterion, paired with a backward elimination, is further adapted to the proposed estimating functions for selecting covariates at a given age. Simulation studies are conducted to examine the proposed approaches regarding consistency, efficiency, and robustness of the estimators. The Firth correction substantially reduces the bias induced by separation and provides valid standard error estimation. We illustrate the proposed approach with the CCSS data viewing premature ovarian insufficiency and surgical premature menopause as the two potential causes of the primary event, premature menopause. The data analysis reveals that the effects of the cancer treatment-related covariates are significant on premature ovarian insufficiency but not on surgical premature menopause. The variable selection procedure, illustrated on an extended covariate set, yields estimated risks close to those under the full model.

Read more
